sourceDefinition: [ Third ]: fem. with p . (T, &c.) The final v in Alv~aAlivu is sometimes changed into Y . (M.) You say, huwa vaAlivu valaAvapK [ He, or it, is the third of three ]: thus you say when the two [terms] agree, each with the other; but not vaAlivN valaAvapF ; vAlv being regarded in the former case as though it were a subst.; for you do not mean to convey by it a verbal signification, but only mean that he, or it, is one of the three, or a portion of the three: (Fr, ISk, T, S:) and in like manner you say, hiYa vaAlivapu valaAva [ She is the third of three ]; but when there is among the females a male, you say, hiYa vaAlivapu valaAvapK , making the masc. to predominate over the fem. (T.) When the two [terms] are different, you may make the former to govern the gen. case or to govern as a verb; saying, huwa raAbiEu valaAvapK or huwa raAbiEN valaAvapF , like as you say DaAribu zayodK and DaAribN zayodFA ; and thus you also say, h`*aA vaAlivu A@vonayoni and h`*aA vaAlivN A@vonayoni , meaning This makes two to be three, with himself, or itself. (ISk, T, * S. [In most copies of the S, for vaAlivN A@vonayoni is put vaAliva A@vonayoni ; and, in the explanation of this phrase, val~ava A@vonayoni for valava A@vonayoni : IB has remarked that these are mistakes.]) ↓ vilaAv occurs in the sense of vaAliv in a trad. cited voce vaAnK in art. vnY . (Sh, T in art. vnY .) ― -b2- vaAlivapu AlA^avaAfiY means A projecting portion of a mountain, by which are placed two pieces of rock, upon all which is placed the cooking-pot. (S, K.) Hence the saying, ramaAhu A@ll~`hu bivaAlivapi AlA^avaAfiY [explained in art. Avf ]. (TA.) ― -b3- [ vaAliva Ea$ara and vaAlivapa Ea$orapa , the former masc. and the latter fem., meaning Thirteenth, are generally held to be indecl. in every case without the art.; but with the art., most say in the nom. Alv~aAlivu Ea$ara , accus. Alv~aAliva Ea$ara , and gen. Alv~aAlivi Ea$ara ; and in like manner in the fem. Accord. to some,] you say, huwa vaAlivu Ea$ara as well as huwa vaAliva Ea$ara [ He, or it, is a thirteenth ]: he who uses the former phrase says that he means huwa vaAlivu valaAvapa Ea$ara , (T, S,) i. e. He, or it, is one of thirteen, (T,) and that he suppresses vlAvh , and leaves vAlv decl. as it was; and he who uses the latter phrase says that he likewise means this, but that, suppressing vlAvp , he gives its final vowel to the word vAlv , (T, S,) to show that there is a suppression: (S:) but IB says that the former of these two phrases is wrong; that the Koofees allow it, but that the Basrees disallow it, and pronounce it a mistake. (L.) [And accord. to J, one says, h`*aA Alv~aAliva Ea$ara and h`*ihi Alv~aAlivapa Ea$orapa This is the thirteenth, or this thirteenth: for he adds,] and you say, h*aA AlHaAdiY Ea$ara and Alv~aAniYa Ea$ara and so on to twenty [exclusive]; all with fet-h; for the reason which we have mentioned: and in like manner in the fem., in which each of the two nouns is with p . (S.) You say also, vaAliva Ea$ara valaAvapa Ea$ara [ The thirteenth of thirteen ]; and so on to taAsiEa Ea$ara tisoEapa Ea$ara : and in like manner in the fem. (I' AK p. 316.)

sourceDefinition: A thing having three angles or corners, triangular [or trilateral ]; a triangle. (S, K.) definition: [The large field-rat;
sourceDefinition: [The large field-rat; so in the present day;] a species of faA^or [or rat ]: (S, A, Mgh, L, K:) or the male fA^r : (T, M, IAmb, L, Msb:) or the large male fA^r ; said to be larger than the jerboa, of a dusky colour, with a blackness in his tail: (L:) or the large fA^r that is in the deserts, or uncultivated plains, and that does not frequent, or keep to, houses: (Msb:) pl. jiro*aAnN , (S, A, Mgh, L, Msb, K,) or juro*aAnN . (TA.) A^kovara A@ll~`hu jiro*aAna bayotika [lit. May God multiply the large rats of thy house, or tent, ] means (tropical:) may God fill thy house, or tent, with wheat, or food. (A.) And tafar~aqato jir*aAnu bayotihi [lit. The large rats of his house, or tent, became dispersed, ] has a contr. meaning. (Har p. 274.) ― -b2- A^um~u jiro*aAnK A sort of dates, (L, Msb, K,) of a large size: before the fruit is cut [from the tree], rats collect beneath: so called when fresh and ripe: when dry, kabiysN : called in El-Koofeh muw$aAnN : (L:) and a sort of palm-tree, the last in the time of the ripening of its fruit in El-Hijáz: (As, AHn, L:) or [simply] the palm-tree. (T in art. Am .) Hence the saying, A_i*aA TalaEati AlxaraAtaAno A^ukilato A^um~u jiro*aAno [ When ElKharátán (the Eleventh Mansion of the Moon) rises aurorally (see manaAzilu Alqamari in art. nzl ), the dates called Am~ jr*An are eaten ]: for El-Khará- tán rises [aurorally] in the last part of the hot season, after the [auroral] rising of suhayol [or Canopus], and before the season called AlS~afariYF . (AHn, L.)

sourceDefinition: A part, or portion, (Msb, K, TA,) or division, (TA,) of a thing; (Msb, TA;) properly and conventionally; (TA;) as also ↓ jazo'N ; (K;) a constituent part of a thing, as of a ship, and of a house or tent, and of a sum in reckoning; (B, TA;) [ an ingredient of any compound or mixture;] a share, or lot: (TA:) pl. A^ajozaA='N : (S, Msb, K, &c. :) it has no other pl. (Sb, TA.) ― -b2- [ A volume of a book.] ― -b3- A foot of a verse. (TA.) ― -b4- In the Kur [xliii. 14], where it is said, wajaEaluwA lahu mino EibaAdihi juzo'FA , (K, TA,) or, as some read, juzu'FA , (Bd,) it means Females; (K, TA;;) i. e., they asserted the angels to be the daughters of God: so says Th: and Aboo-Is-hák says that it means, they asserted God's share of offspring to be the females; but that he had not found this in old poetry, nor had persons worthy of confidence related it on the authority of the Arabs [of the classical times]: Z disallows it, asserting it to be a lie against the Arabs; and Bd follows him: El-Khafájee says that the word may be used figuratively; for, as Eve was created of a part ( juzo' ) of Adam, the word jz' may be applied to denote the female. (MF, TA.)

sourceDefinition: What is cast forth [ of froth, or foam, and particles of rubbish or refuse, (see 1,)] by a torrent: (ISk, S:) the froth, or foam, cast forth by a valley [ flowing with water ]; and by a cooking-pot, (K, TA,) in boiling. (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, as being likened to the froth, or foam, of the cooking-pot, of which no use is made, (Fr, TA,) i. q. baATilN [meaning A thing that is worthless, useless, or unprofitable ]. (Fr, K, TA.) It is said in the Kur [xiii. 18], faA^am~aA Alz~abadu faya*ohabu jufaA='F , meaning baATilFA [i. e. Now as to the froth, or scum, it passeth away as a thing that is worthless, or useless, or unprofitable ], (Fr, S, Jel, TA,) and thrown away. (Jel.) You say also, *ahaba Alz~abadu jufaA='F , meaning [ The froth, or scum, passed away ] driven from its water. definition: The yad (S, K) [meaning wing ] of a bird or flying thing;
sourceDefinition: The yad (S, K) [meaning wing ] of a bird or flying thing; (S;) i. e., of a bird or flying thing, the limb that corresponds to the yd of a man: (Msb:) and also the yd [i. e. arm, sometimes also meaning hand, (see a signification of janaHa ,)] of a man: (L, TA:) and (K) the upper arm, or arm from the shoulder to the elbow: (Zj, L, K:) each of these is so called because it is on one side of the body: (L:) and the armpit: (K:) pl. A^ajoniHapN (S, Msb, K) and A^ajonuHN : (IJ, K:) the sing., though masc., has the latter pl., which properly belongs to a fem. sing. [of this form], because jnAH is assimilated to riy$apN ; (IJ;) [or rather, I think, to yadN , which is fem.;] but some assert jnAH to be both masc. and fem. (MF.) [Hence,] huwa maqoSuwSu AljanaAHi [ He has the wing clipped; meaning] (tropical:) he is one who lacks strength or power or ability; he is impotent. (A, TA.) And xafaDa lahu janaAHahu (tropical:) [ He abased himself to him: lit. he lowered to him his wing: but see an explanation of a similar phrase in the Kur, below]. (A.) And rakibuwA janaAHaYi AlT~aAy^iri , (Fr, L, K,) in [some of the copies of] the K, AlT~ariyqi , (TA,) (assumed tropical:) They quitted their homes, or accustomed places. (Fr, L, K.) And fulaAnN fiY janaAHaYo TaAy^irK Such a one is in a state of disquiet, and confounded, or perplexed, unable to see his right course. (L, A. *) And rakiba fulaAnN janaAHaYi Aln~aEaAmapi (tropical:) Such a one employed himself vigorously, labouriously, sedulously, or diligently, in an affair; (A, K;) managing well. (K.) And naHonu EalaY janaAHi Als~afari [lit. We are on the wing of travel; meaning] (tropical:) we are about to travel, or journey. (K, TA.) And janaAHu Alfarasi (assumed tropical:) A certain star [ γ ] of Pegasus; one of the four bright stars, in Pegasus, which form a square; the other three being that at the extremity of the neck, called Eayonu Alfarasi , [i. e. a of Pegasus,] that called manokibu Alfarasi , [ β of Pegasus,] and the star [ a of Andromeda] that belongs to both Pegasus and Andromeda. (Kzw.) [And janaAHu samakapK (assumed tropical:) The fin of a fish. ] And janaAHaA naSolK (assumed tropical:) The two wings, or blades, of a spear-head or of an arrow-head. (L.) And janaAHu Alr~aHaY (assumed tropical:) The wing ( naAEuwr ) of the mill or mill-stone. (L.) And janaAHaA EasokarK (tropical:) The two wings of an army. (A, TA) And janaAHaA AlwaAdiY (tropical:) The two sides of the valley (A, L) down which the water runs, on the right and left. (L.) And variydapN lahaA janaAHaAni mino EuraAqK and biAlEuraAqi ↓ mujan~aHapN (tropical:) [ A mess of crumbled bread moistened with broth, having two sidegarnishes of bones with some meat remaining upon them ]. (A, TA.) ― -b2- See also jinoHN , in two places. ― -b3- Also The side, syn. jaAnibN . (K.) So in the saying in the Kur [xvii. 25], waA@xofiDo lahumaA janaAHa Al*~ul~i , meaning waA^alino lahumaA jaAnibaka Al*~aliyla (tropical:) [ And make soft to them [thy two parents) thy submissive side; i. e. treat them with gentleness and submissiveness: or the former words may be literally rendered lower to them the wing of submissiveness; meaning be submissive to them ]. (Jel, TA.) ― -b4- And A part, or portion, of a thing; as also ↓ junaAHN . (K.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yajuwdu , inf. n. juwdapN and jawodapN , It (a thing, S, or a commodity, an article of household-goods, or the like, Msb, and a work, or performance, TA) was, or became, jay~id [i. e. good, goodly, approvable, or excellent; the verb being the contr. of raduw^a , as is implied in the A and K]: (S, A, Msb, K:) in this sense, accord. to some, of the class of qaAla ; accord. to others, of the class of qaruba . (Msb.) [Also said of a man, meaning He was, or became, excellent, or egregious, in some quality; sometimes, though very rarely, in a quality that is disapproved.] ― -b2- And jAd , (S, A, Msb, K,) of the class of qAl , (Msb,) aor. as above, (S, Msb,) inf. n. juwdN , (S, A, Msb, K,) with damm, (S, Msb,) He was liberal, bountiful, munificent, or generous: (K:) or he affected, or constrained himself, to be generous: (Msb:) or he gave without being asked, to preserve the receiver from the ignominy of asking: (MF:) or he gave what was meet to him to whom it was meet: (El-Karmánee, TA:) or he gave what was meet to him to whom it was meet, not for a compensation; so that it has a more special signification than A^aHosana . (MF.) You say, jAd bimaAlihi [ He was liberal, &c., with his property ]: (S:) or jAd biAlmaAli he affected, or constrained himself, to be generous with the property. (Msb.) ― -b3- Hence, (Msb,) jAd binafosihi , (S, Msb, K,) aor. as above, (S, A,) inf. n. jawodN (TA) and juw^uwdN , (S, TA,) (tropical:) He gave up his spirit, (A, Msb, TA,) at death; (S, Msb;) like as one gives away his property; said of one in the agony of death: (TA:) and (tropical:) he gave away his life, in war. (Msb.) And you say also, jaAdato nafosuhu (assumed tropical:) [ His soul, or spirit, resigned itself, or departed ]. (Msb in art. nfs .) ― -b4- jAd AlmaTaru , inf. n. jawodN , The rain was, or became, copious, or abundant. (S.) And jaAdati Als~amaA='u , (A, Msb,) inf. n. jawodN , with fet-h, The sky rained. (Msb.) And jaAdati AlEayonu , inf. n. jawodN and juw^uwdN , The eye shed many, or abundant, tears. (Lh, K.) ― -b5- jAd said of a horse, (S, A, L, Msb, K,) aor. as above, (S,) inf. n. juwdapN (S, L, Msb, K) and jawodapN ; (Msb, and some copies of the K;) and ↓ jwd , (A, L, K,) inf. n. tajowiydN ; (TA;) and ↓ AjAd , (L,) and ↓ A^ajowada ; (L, K;) He became fleet, or swift, and excellent, (L,) SaAra raAy^iEFA , (S, L, K, *) fiY Eadowihi in his running. (A, L, K.) [See an ex. in a verse cited voce daAma , in art. dwm .] ― -b6- See also 4, in two places. ― -b7- jAd A_ilayohi He inclined to him, or it. (TA.) -A2- jAdhu He overcame him in liberality, bounty, munificence, or generosity. (K.) See 3. ― -b2- jaAdahumo , aor. yajuwdu , inf. n. jawodN , It (rain) rained, or descended, upon them copiously, or abundantly. (L.) And jiyduwA They were rained upon with a copious, or an abundant, rain. (L.) And jiydati AlA^aroDu , (S, L, K,) inf. n. jawodN ; (As, TA;) and ↓ A^ujiydat ; (K;) The earth, or land, was rained upon with a copious, or an abundant, rain: (S, L, K:) or, so that the moisture of the rain met that of the soil. definition: He chose what was good, goodly, approvable, or excellent, among all things.
sourceDefinition: He chose what was good, goodly, approvable, or excellent, among all things. (Ham p. 299.) definition: Copious, or abundant, rain;
sourceDefinition: Copious, or abundant, rain; (S, L, K;) as also ↓ jaAy^idN : (S:) or rain that thoroughly irrigates everything: (M:) or rain that is not exceeded: (M, L, K:) accord. to some, who observe that the phrase, mentioned by Sb, A^axa*otanaA biAljawodiwafawoqhaA [ Thou hast assailed us with a storm of reproach or the like not to be exceeded, and with that which is above it, ] is one of hyperbole and reproach. (M, L.) It is an inf. n. thus used as an epithet [and therefore applicable without variation to a fem. as to a masc. n., and to a dual and a pl. as to a sing. n.]: (L:) and is also pl. [or rather a quasi-pl. n.] of jaAy^idN , (S, L, K,) like as SaHobN is of SaAHibN . (S, L.) You say maTarN jawodN [ A copious, or an abundant, rain; &c.]: (L:) and saHaAbapN jawodN [ A cloud yielding a copious, or an abundant, rain; &c.]: (IAar, L:) and haAjato lanaA samaA='N jawodN [ A copious, or an abundant, rain, &c., became stirred up for us ]: (S, K: *) and you also say, [contr. to the usage mentioned above, or as though jawodN were an epithet from jaAda , and this originally jawoda , like DaxomN from Daxuma , but used as a subst.,] maTorataAni jawodaAni [ Two showers of rain, copious, or abundant, &c.]. (S, K.) ↓ tajaAwiydu , [app. signifying the same as jawodN used as a pl.,] occurring in the following verse of Sakhr El-Ghei, yulaAEibu Alr~iyHa biAlEaSorayoni qaSoTaluhu waAlwaAbiluwna watahotaAnu Alt~ajaAwiydi [ Its dust makes sport with the wind in the morning and evening, or night and day, and so do the violent showers of big drops, and the pouring of copious, or abundant, rains, &c.], (L, K, *) is a pl. having no sing.; (K;) or it may be so, like taEaAjiybu and taEaA$iybu and tabaA$iyru ; or it may be pl. of tajowaAdN [an inf. n.]. (L.) You say also, AmaTari ↓ A^aSaAbatohu tajaAwiydu [ Copious showers of rain fell upon him, or it ]. (A.) ― -b2- See also jawaAdN .

definition: , originally of the measure fayoEilN , (S, Msb,) as the Basrees say, i.
sourceDefinition: , originally of the measure fayoEilN , (S, Msb,) as the Basrees say, i. e. jayowidN , (Msb, TA,) the w being changed into Y because of its being meksoor and preceded by Y , and the augmentative Y being then incorporated into it; (TA;) or, as the Koofees say, of the measure fayoEalN , like EayoTalN &c., because there is found no sound word of the measure fayoEilN except SayoqilN , a woman's name, and the unsound is accorded to the sound; or, as others say, of the measure faEiylN , [and so I find in one copy of the S,] originally jawiydN , the kesreh of the w being, accord. to them, suppressed because difficult of pronunciation, and the quiescent w and Y thus coming together, [the latter receives the rejected kesreh, and] the w is changed into Y and incorporated into the [augmentative] Y ; (Msb;) Good, goodly, approvable, or excellent; contr. of radi Yo ; (A, K;) applied to a thing, (S,) or a commodity, an article of household-goods, or the like, (A, Msb,) and a work, or performance: (TA:) pl. jiyaAdN (S, A, Msb, K) and jiyaAdaAtN , (K,) the latter a pl. pl., [i. e. pl. of jiyaAdN ,] (TA,) and jayaAy^idu , (S, K,) with hemz, [and, accord. to some,] contr. to analogy. (S.) [It is also applied to a man, meaning Excellent, or egregious, in some quality; sometimes, though very rarely, in a quality that is disapproved.]

sourceDefinition: : see HutaAt . ― -b2- Also Dead; [as though strewn upon the ground, in fragments;] applied to locusts ( jaraAd ): pl. A^aHotaAtN ; (K;) its only pl. (MF.) [See also Huv~N .] ― -b4- (tropical:) A fleet, or swift, horse; (S, A;) as though he scraped the ground; (A;) light in pace, and wide in step: pl. as above: (S:) or a fleet, or swift, and excellent horse; (K;) that runs swiftly and much, or that furrows the ground much with his feet: (TA:) also generous and high-bred ( kariymN EatiyqN [app. as applied to a horse]): (K:) and a fleet, or swift, camel: (K:) a quick-paced and light-paced camel; as also ↓ HatoHatN : (TA:) and a male ostrich. (K.) The Hudhalee says, (S,) namely, El-Aalam, (TA,) ElY Hat~i AlburaAyapi zamoxariY~i Also sawaAEidi Zal~a fiY $aroYK TiwaAli (S, TA:) he likens himself, says As, in his running and fleeing, to a male ostrich, as is shown by what precedes this verse: (S:) by Ht~ AlbrAyp is said to be meant Hat~K Einoda AlburaAyapi , i. e. (tropical:) fleet, or swift, when emaciated by journeying; the subst. brAyp being said to be put for the inf. n. baroY : (A, * L:) some of the Basrees say that the poet means a camel; but As disapproves of this, because to that which he here describes he has before applied the epithet hijaf~ : ISd says that in his opinion he likens his horse or his camel to a male ostrich, because of the epithet hjf~ , preceding, and because neither the horse nor the camel eats the colocynth, but this plant is cropped by ostriches; $rY meaning the colocynth: IJ says that $rY here signifies a tree of which bows are made; and the poet means that if the trees thus called are tall, they conceal him, and he is the more lonesome, or sad; and that if they were short, his eye would range freely, and he would be pleased, and would run gently. (L.) -A2- See also Hat~aY , near the end of the paragraph.

definition: is a particle, used in three senses: (Mughnee:) it is a particle denoting the end of an extent;
sourceDefinition: is a particle, used in three senses: (Mughnee:) it is a particle denoting the end of an extent; (Mughnee, K;) which is its predominant meaning; (Mughnee;) asserted by some to be always its meaning: (TA:) and denoting a cause, or motive: and syn. with A_il~aA as an exceptive; (Mughnee, K;) which last is the rarest, and is mentioned by few. (Mughnee.) ― -b2- It is used as a preposition governing the gen. case, in the same manner as A_ilaY (S, Mughnee) in respect of meaning and government, (Mughnee,) denoting the end of an extent; (S;) [signifying To, till, until, or to the time of; ] but the word that it so governs must be a noun properly so called, not a pronoun except in a case of poetic license; and must signify the last part, or portion, of what is signified by that which precedes Ht~Y , as in the saying, A^akalotu Als~amakapa Hat~aY raA^osihaA [ I ate the fish, even to its head ]; or must be prefixed to the word signifying that part, or portion, as in the saying, [in the Kur xcvii. last verse,] salaAmN hiYa Hat~aY maTolaEi Alfajori [A night of peace, or of salutation, is it, until the time of the rising of the dawn ]. (Mughnee.) It is also followed by a mansoob aor., as in sirotu Hat~aY A^adoxulahaA [ I journeyed until I entered it, AdxlhA here virtually meaning daxalotuhaA ], A^ano being here understood after Ht~Y , and the An together with the verb being rendered in grammatical analysis by an inf. n. governed in the gen. case by Ht~Y [so that Ht~Y An AdxlhA means Ht~Y duxuwliY A_iy~aAhaA ]: this is one of the cases in which Ht~Y differs from A_ilaY ; for one may not say, sirotu A_ilaY A^adoxulahaA [with A^ano understood after AlY ]: and in the same sense it is used in the phrase, [in the Kur xx. 93,] Hat~aY yarojiEa A_ilayonaA muwsaY [ Until Moses return to us ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b3- It is also syn. with kaYo , denoting a cause or motive [of action &c., signifying To the end that, in order that, or so that ], as in the saying, A^asolimo Hat~aY tadoxula Aljan~apa [ Become a Muslim, to the end that, or in order that, or so that, thou mayest enter Paradise ]; being in this case, likewise, followed by a mansoob aor. (Mughnee.) ― -b4- It is also used [as a preposition virtually governing the gen. case, A^ano being understood after it,] in the sense of A_il~aA , meaning Except, or unless, likewise followed by a mansoob aor., as in the following verse: layosa AlEaTaA='u mina AlfuDuwli samaAHapF Hat~aY tajuwda wamaA ladayoka qaliylu [ The giving of superfluities is not liberality: (giving is not liberality) except, or unless, (or here we may also say until, ) thou be bountiful when little is in thy possession ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b5- It is also a conjunction, like wa , [signifying And, or rather even, ] (S, Mughnee,) but on three conditions: first, that the word following it and conjoined by it be a noun properly so called, not a pronoun: secondly, that this noun signify a part, or portion, of what is signified by that which precedes Ht~Y , as in qadima AlHuj~aAju Hat~aY Almu$aApu [ The pilgrims arrived: even those on foot ], and A^akalotu Als~amakapa Hat~Y raA^osahaA [ I ate the fish: even its head ]: thirdly, that the noun following it and conjoined by it denote either the greatest or the least [literally or figuratively] of what are included in the signification of the noun that precedes Ht~Y , as in maAta Aln~aAsu Hat~aY AlA^anobiyaA='u [ Men have died: even the prophets ], and zaAraka Aln~aAsu Hat~aY AlHaj~aAmuwna [ The people visited thee: even the cuppers ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b6- It is also used as an inceptive particle, (S, Mughnee,) preceding a nominal proposition, (Mughnee,) as in the following verse (of Jereer [so in a copy of the S]): famaA zaAlati AlqatolaY tamuj~a dimaA='ahaA bidijolapa Hat~aY maA='u dijolapa A^a$okalu [ And the slain ceased not to emit their blood into the Tigris, so that the water of the Tigris was of a mixed colour consisting of red and white ]: (S, Mughnee:) and preceding a verbal proposition, of which the verb is a pret., as in the phrase, [in the Kur vii. 93,] Hat~aY EafawoA waqaAluwA [ So that they became numerous, and said ]: (Mughnee:) and preceding a marfooa aor., as in the phrase, [in the Kur ii. 210,] Hat~aY yaquwlu Alr~asuwlu [ So that the Apostle said, or, as in the S, so that this was the case: the Apostle said ], accord. to him who reads yaquwlu ; (IHsh, in De Sacy's “ Anthol. Gramm. Ar., ” p. 82 of the Arabic text;) others reading yaquwla , which, as well as yaquwlu , here means qaAla . (Jel.) ― -b7- [Respecting the cases in which the mansoob aor. is used after HA~Y , and those in which the marfooa aor. is used, the following observations are made.] When Ht~Y precedes a future, the latter is mansoob, by reason of A^ano understood before it, as in the saying, sirotu A_ilY Alkuwfapi Hat~aY A^adoxulahaA [ I journeyed to El-Koofeh until I entered it: see above]: (S:) it is not mansoob unless the verb is a future: if it is future with respect to the time of speaking, it must be mansoob, as in Hat~aY yarojiEa A_ilayonaA muwsaY [cited above]: if the verb is future with respect to what precedes, only, it may be mansoob, as in Hat~aY yaquwla Alr~asuwlu [mentioned above]; or it may be marfooa; but not unless [somehow] denoting a present time; (Mughnee;) and if present with respect to the time of speaking, it must be marfooa, as in the saying, sirotu A_ilaY Alkuwfapi Hat~aY A^adoxuluhaA [ I have journeyed to El-Koofeh so that now I am entering it ]; (S, Mughnee; *) but if not really present, it is not marfooa unless denoting a past event as though it were present, as in Hat~aY yaquwlu Alr~asuwlu [explained above]; nor may it be marfooa unless denoting an effect of what precedes it; so that you may not say, sirotu Hat~aY taToluEu Al$~amosu , nor maA sirotu Hat~aY A^adoxuluhaA unless the mA is regarded as prefixed to the entire affirmative phrase that follows it, nor halo sirota Hat~aY tadoxuluhaA ; nor may it be marfooa unless it denote a complement to what precedes it, so that you may not say syorY Hat~aY A^adoxuluhaA , as the inchoative would in this case be without an enunciative. (Mughnee.) ― -b8- [The following verse of El-Farezdak is cited in the Mughnee as an ex. of Ht~Y used as an inceptive particle: fawaAEajabaA Hat~aY kulayobN tasub~uniY kaA^an~a A^abaAhaA naho$alN wamujaA$iEu and it is there added that yasub~uniY Aln~aAsu must be understood in this verse before Ht~Y : but I rather think that Ht~Y is here a conjunctive particle, and that the meaning is, And alas, my wonder! the people revile me: even Kuleyb revile me, as though their father were Nahshal and as though he were Mujáshi'. ] ― -b9- It should be observed that Ht~uY may be used in three different ways in some sentences: thus you may say, using it as a preposition (in the sense of A_ilaY ), A^akalotu Als~amakapa Hat~aY raA^osihaA [ I ate the fish, even to its head ]; and, using it as a conjunction, Hat~aY raA^osahaA [ even its head ]; and, using it as an inceptive particle, Hat~aY raA^osuhaA [for Hat~aY raA^osuhaA maA^okuwlN so that its head was eaten ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b10- It is said in the K that Ht~Y renders makhfood and marfooa and mansoob; and that therefore Fr said, A^amuwtu wafiY nafosiY mino Hat~aY $aYo'N [“ I shall die with something respecting Ht~Y (remaining unsettled) in my mind ”]: this is said on the supposition that Ht~Y deviates in government from an established rule, which is, that a particle which governs one part of speech governs that only; those, for instance, which render mansoob and mejzoom governing verbs only, and the particles that govern nouns governing none but nouns: but the truth is, that Ht~Y governs only the gen. case; a marfooa noun or aor. after it would be so without it, as Ht~Y in this case is only an inceptive particle; and a mansoob aor. after it is rendered so by A^ano understood, so that Ht~Y in this case virtually governs a noun in the gen. case [as has been shown above]: therefore the remark quoted above from the K is faulty, and confounds things that should be distinguished. (MF, TA.) ― -b11- Some say that Ht~Y is [a noun] of the measure faEolaY , from ↓ AlHat~u the ceasing from a thing, having finished it; or the becoming unoccupied by a thing; like $at~aY from Al$~at~u : but Az disapproves of this, because, were it so, the pronunciation termed A_imaAlap would be allowable in its case, and it is not so: Ht~Y , he says, is a particle, not a noun, nor a verb. (TA.) ― -b12- Hat~aAma is originally Hat~aY maA [ Till when? until when? or how long? ]: the A of mA is elided because the expression is used interrogatively, like as it is when any preposition is prefixed to it if used interrogatively, as in bima and fiyma and Eam~a . (S.) ― -b13- In the dial. of Hudheyl, Eat~aY is said for Hat~aY . (L.)

(Mughnee.) ― -b2- It is used as a preposition governing the gen. case, in the same manner as A_ilaY (S, Mughnee) in respect of meaning and government, (Mughnee,) denoting the end of an extent; (S;) [signifying To, till, until, or to the time of; ] but the word that it so governs must be a noun properly so called, not a pronoun except in a case of poetic license; and must signify the last part, or portion, of what is signified by that which precedes Ht~Y , as in the saying, A^akalotu Als~amakapa Hat~aY raA^osihaA [ I ate the fish, even to its head ]; or must be prefixed to the word signifying that part, or portion, as in the saying, [in the Kur xcvii. last verse,] salaAmN hiYa Hat~aY maTolaEi Alfajori [A night of peace, or of salutation, is it, until the time of the rising of the dawn ]. (Mughnee.) It is also followed by a mansoob aor., as in sirotu Hat~aY A^adoxulahaA [ I journeyed until I entered it, AdxlhA here virtually meaning daxalotuhaA ], A^ano being here understood after Ht~Y , and the An together with the verb being rendered in grammatical analysis by an inf. n. governed in the gen. case by Ht~Y [so that Ht~Y An AdxlhA means Ht~Y duxuwliY A_iy~aAhaA ]: this is one of the cases in which Ht~Y differs from A_ilaY ; for one may not say, sirotu A_ilaY A^adoxulahaA [with A^ano understood after AlY ]: and in the same sense it is used in the phrase, [in the Kur xx. 93,] Hat~aY yarojiEa A_ilayonaA muwsaY [ Until Moses return to us ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b3- It is also syn. with kaYo , denoting a cause or motive [of action &c., signifying To the end that, in order that, or so that ], as in the saying, A^asolimo Hat~aY tadoxula Aljan~apa [ Become a Muslim, to the end that, or in order that, or so that, thou mayest enter Paradise ]; being in this case, likewise, followed by a mansoob aor. (Mughnee.) ― -b4- It is also used [as a preposition virtually governing the gen. case, A^ano being understood after it,] in the sense of A_il~aA , meaning Except, or unless, likewise followed by a mansoob aor., as in the following verse: layosa AlEaTaA='u mina AlfuDuwli samaAHapF Hat~aY tajuwda wamaA ladayoka qaliylu [ The giving of superfluities is not liberality: (giving is not liberality) except, or unless, (or here we may also say until, ) thou be bountiful when little is in thy possession ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b5- It is also a conjunction, like wa , [signifying And, or rather even, ] (S, Mughnee,) but on three conditions: first, that the word following it and conjoined by it be a noun properly so called, not a pronoun: secondly, that this noun signify a part, or portion, of what is signified by that which precedes Ht~Y , as in qadima AlHuj~aAju Hat~aY Almu$aApu [ The pilgrims arrived: even those on foot ], and A^akalotu Als~amakapa Hat~Y raA^osahaA [ I ate the fish: even its head ]: thirdly, that the noun following it and conjoined by it denote either the greatest or the least [literally or figuratively] of what are included in the signification of the noun that precedes Ht~Y , as in maAta Aln~aAsu Hat~aY AlA^anobiyaA='u [ Men have died: even the prophets ], and zaAraka Aln~aAsu Hat~aY AlHaj~aAmuwna [ The people visited thee: even the cuppers ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b6- It is also used as an inceptive particle, (S, Mughnee,) preceding a nominal proposition, (Mughnee,) as in the following verse (of Jereer [so in a copy of the S]): famaA zaAlati AlqatolaY tamuj~a dimaA='ahaA bidijolapa Hat~aY maA='u dijolapa A^a$okalu [ And the slain ceased not to emit their blood into the Tigris, so that the water of the Tigris was of a mixed colour consisting of red and white ]: (S, Mughnee:) and preceding a verbal proposition, of which the verb is a pret., as in the phrase, [in the Kur vii. 93,] Hat~aY EafawoA waqaAluwA [ So that they became numerous, and said ]: (Mughnee:) and preceding a marfooa aor., as in the phrase, [in the Kur ii. 210,] Hat~aY yaquwlu Alr~asuwlu [ So that the Apostle said, or, as in the S, so that this was the case: the Apostle said ], accord. to him who reads yaquwlu ; (IHsh, in De Sacy's “ Anthol. Gramm. Ar., ” p. 82 of the Arabic text;) others reading yaquwla , which, as well as yaquwlu , here means qaAla . (Jel.) ― -b7- [Respecting the cases in which the mansoob aor. is used after HA~Y , and those in which the marfooa aor. is used, the following observations are made.] When Ht~Y precedes a future, the latter is mansoob, by reason of A^ano understood before it, as in the saying, sirotu A_ilY Alkuwfapi Hat~aY A^adoxulahaA [ I journeyed to El-Koofeh until I entered it: see above]: (S:) it is not mansoob unless the verb is a future: if it is future with respect to the time of speaking, it must be mansoob, as in Hat~aY yarojiEa A_ilayonaA muwsaY [cited above]: if the verb is future with respect to what precedes, only, it may be mansoob, as in Hat~aY yaquwla Alr~asuwlu [mentioned above]; or it may be marfooa; but not unless [somehow] denoting a present time; (Mughnee;) and if present with respect to the time of speaking, it must be marfooa, as in the saying, sirotu A_ilaY Alkuwfapi Hat~aY A^adoxuluhaA [ I have journeyed to El-Koofeh so that now I am entering it ]; (S, Mughnee; *) but if not really present, it is not marfooa unless denoting a past event as though it were present, as in Hat~aY yaquwlu Alr~asuwlu [explained above]; nor may it be marfooa unless denoting an effect of what precedes it; so that you may not say, sirotu Hat~aY taToluEu Al$~amosu , nor maA sirotu Hat~aY A^adoxuluhaA unless the mA is regarded as prefixed to the entire affirmative phrase that follows it, nor halo sirota Hat~aY tadoxuluhaA ; nor may it be marfooa unless it denote a complement to what precedes it, so that you may not say syorY Hat~aY A^adoxuluhaA , as the inchoative would in this case be without an enunciative. (Mughnee.) ― -b8- [The following verse of El-Farezdak is cited in the Mughnee as an ex. of Ht~Y used as an inceptive particle: fawaAEajabaA Hat~aY kulayobN tasub~uniY kaA^an~a A^abaAhaA naho$alN wamujaA$iEu and it is there added that yasub~uniY Aln~aAsu must be understood in this verse before Ht~Y : but I rather think that Ht~Y is here a conjunctive particle, and that the meaning is, And alas, my wonder! the people revile me: even Kuleyb revile me, as though their father were Nahshal and as though he were Mujáshi'. ] ― -b9- It should be observed that Ht~uY may be used in three different ways in some sentences: thus you may say, using it as a preposition (in the sense of A_ilaY ), A^akalotu Als~amakapa Hat~aY raA^osihaA [ I ate the fish, even to its head ]; and, using it as a conjunction, Hat~aY raA^osahaA [ even its head ]; and, using it as an inceptive particle, Hat~aY raA^osuhaA [for Hat~aY raA^osuhaA maA^okuwlN so that its head was eaten ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b10- It is said in the K that Ht~Y renders makhfood and marfooa and mansoob; and that therefore Fr said, A^amuwtu wafiY nafosiY mino Hat~aY $aYo'N [“ I shall die with something respecting Ht~Y (remaining unsettled) in my mind ”]: this is said on the supposition that Ht~Y deviates in government from an established rule, which is, that a particle which governs one part of speech governs that only; those, for instance, which render mansoob and mejzoom governing verbs only, and the particles that govern nouns governing none but nouns: but the truth is, that Ht~Y governs only the gen. case; a marfooa noun or aor. after it would be so without it, as Ht~Y in this case is only an inceptive particle; and a mansoob aor. after it is rendered so by A^ano understood, so that Ht~Y in this case virtually governs a noun in the gen. case [as has been shown above]: therefore the remark quoted above from the K is faulty, and confounds things that should be distinguished. (MF, TA.) ― -b11- Some say that Ht~Y is [a noun] of the measure faEolaY , from ↓ AlHat~u the ceasing from a thing, having finished it; or the becoming unoccupied by a thing; like $at~aY from Al$~at~u : but Az disapproves of this, because, were it so, the pronunciation termed A_imaAlap would be allowable in its case, and it is not so: Ht~Y , he says, is a particle, not a noun, nor a verb. (TA.) ― -b12- Hat~aAma is originally Hat~aY maA [ Till when? until when? or how long? ]: the A of mA is elided because the expression is used interrogatively, like as it is when any preposition is prefixed to it if used interrogatively, as in bima and fiyma and Eam~a . (S.) ― -b13- In the dial. of Hudheyl, Eat~aY is said for Hat~aY . (L.)

definition: Deprived of an arm, or a hand, &c.
sourceDefinition: Deprived of an arm, or a hand, &c., by amputation: fem. Ha*~aA='u : [pl. Hu*~N :] thus A^aHa*~u Alyadi means having the arm, or hand, amputated: and [hence] (assumed tropical:) not having the means of acquiring eminence, or nobility. (L.) [Hence, also,] A^aSuwlu biyadK Ha*~aA='a , in a trad. of 'Alee, means (assumed tropical:) Shall I assault the enemy with a short arm, that will not attain to that which I desire? or, accord. to one reading, it is ja*~aA='a , meaning amputated: alluding to his companions' falling short of their duty, and keeping back from the war. (L in arts. H* and j* .) [Another meaning of A^aHa*~u Alyadi will be found below.] ― -b2- A light-tailed camel: (S, L:) a horse light, or scanty, in the hair of the tail: (A, L:) or having it ( the tail, Msb) cut off: (A, Msb:) a short-tailed ass. (L.) qaTaApN Ha*~aA='u A bird of the kind called qaTFA having a light, or scanty, tail; having a tail of which the feathers have become light, or scanty; (S, L;) having few feathers in the tail: (A:) or short-tailed: (L:) or (assumed tropical:) light and quick in flight. (A, * L.) And liHoyapN Ha*~aA='u A light, or scanty, beard. (L.) ― -b3- Lean, lank, or light of flesh; or slender; or lank in the belly. (K.) ― -b4- Smooth; (Kh, Msb;) a thing to which nothing clings, or attaches. (Msb, * TA.) wal~ati Ald~unoyaA Ha*~aA='a , in a xuTobap of 'Otbeh Ibn-Ghazwán, means (tropical:) The world hath retired, passing away quickly, (A, * L, K *) nothing clinging to it [ so as to retard it ]: (L, K:) or the people thereof not clinging to aught of it [ so as to retard it ]: (A:) or quickly; its latter part being cut off. (Az, L.) ― -b5- A sword quick in cutting. (A.) ― -b6- (tropical:) Light-handed; (S, A, L, K;) quick-handed; (L;) i. e. thievish; or quick in getting, or attaining: (A:) [and so A^aHa*~u Alyadi , as is implied in the S and L.] El-Farezdak uses the expression A^aHa*~a yadi AlqamiySi , (S, L,) meaning thereby A^aHa*~a Alyadi . (L.) naAqapN Ha*~aA='u (assumed tropical:) A she-camel quick in pace. (A.) ― -b7- qalobN A^aHa*~u (assumed tropical:) A sharp, quick, active mind. (L.) ― -b8- sayorN A^aHa*~u (tropical:) A very quick, unpleasant journey or pace. (A.) See also Ha*oHaA*N . ― -b9- A^amorN A^aHa*~u (tropical:) An affair, or event, quick in passing: (L:) or decisive and quick: (TA:) or severe and abominable; (A, L, K;) without a parallel: (A:) or as though it eluded every one, so that he could not attain to it, and was not sufficient for it: (A:) pl. Hu*~N . (L, K.) ― -b10- yamiynN Ha*~aA='u (tropical:) An oath which a man takes quickly: (S, K:) or an abominable, severe oath, whereby one decides a right, or due: (A, L:) some say ja*~aA='u . (S.) (A, L.) ― -b13- raHimN Ha*~aA='u (tropical:) A bond of relationship [ cut, or severed, or] not made close by affection; expl. by A_i*aA lamo tuwSalo : (Fr, S, K:) as also ja*~aA=' [q. v.]. (Fr, S.) ― -b14- A^aHa*~u A^aba*~u : see ba*~N .

definition: War, battle, fight, or conflict;
sourceDefinition: War, battle, fight, or conflict; (Msb, TA;) contr. of silomN ; (TA;) consisting, first, in shooting arrows, one at another; then, in thrusting, one at another, with spears; then, in combating one another with swords; and then, in grappling and struggling together: (Suh, TA:) it is [generally] fem.; (S, L Msb;) but its dim. is ↓ HurayobN , without p , (Kh, S, L, Msb,) contr. to rule, (L, Msb,) like *urayoEN , and quwayosN , and furayosN in a fem. sense, (L,) because originally an inf. n. [of which the verb ( Haraba ) seems not to have been used as meaning “ he waged, or contended in, war ”], (El-Mázinee, S,) or in order that it may not be confounded with the dim. of HarobapN : (Msb:) Seer makes its origin to be the epithet HarobN , which, however, is originally an inf. n.: (L:) sometimes it is masc.; (IAar, Mbr, S, Msb, K;) but this is extr.: (L:) the pl. is HuruwbN . (S, K.) You say, waqaEato bayonahumo HarobN [ War happened between them ]. (S.) And qaAmati AlHarobu EalaY saAqK The war, or battle, became vehement, so that safety from destruction was difficult of attainment. (Msb.) And making it masc., as meaning qitaAlN , you say HarobN $adiydN A vehement fight or battle. (Msb.) [Hence,] Aibonu HarobK A warrior: (Er-Rághib, TA in art. bnY :) and Aibonu AlHarobi [ the warrior; or] he who suffices for war, and who defends. (Msb in that art.) And daAru AlHarobi The country, or countries, of the unbelievers, (Msb,) or of [ those called by the Muslims ] the polytheists, (K,) between whom and the Muslims there is not peace. (Msb, K.) In the saying of Aboo- Haneefeh, kaAnato mak~apu A_i*o *`Aka HarobFA , the meaning is daAra HarobK [ Mekkeh was at that time a place of which the people were at war with the Muslims ]. (Mgh.) -A2- It is also an epithet; originally an inf. n. (L.) You say rajulN HarobN , (K, TA,) [in the CK HaribN , but it is] like EadolN , (TA,) A man vehement in war, and courageous; as also ↓ miHorabN and ↓ miHoraAbN : (K:) or ↓ miHorabN signifies a man of wars; (S;) or a man of war, as also ↓ miHoraAbN ; and a known, experienced warrior. (TA.) [Being originally an inf. n.,] HarobN as an epithet is used in the same form as masc. and fem. and sing. and pl.: (K:) so that one says AimoraA^apN HarobN and qawomN HarobN , (TA,) as also ↓ qawomN miHorabapN . (S, K.) ― -b2- Also An enemy, (S, K,) whether, or not, actually at war. (K.) So in the saying, A^anaA HarobN limano HaArabanaYi [ I am an enemy to him who wars with me, or who is an enemy to me ]. (S.) And fulaAnN Harobu fulaAnK Such a one is the enemy of such a one. (TA.) Some hold that HarobN is a pl. [or rather a quasi-pl. n.] of HaAribN or muHaAribN . (TA.)

sourceDefinition: inf. n. of Hariba . (A, Mgh, Msb.) waAHarabaA is an ejaculation expressive of grief, lamentation, or regret, [meaning Alas, my spoliation! or my loss! or my grief! ] (ISd, Mgh, TA,) used in an absolute manner, like waA A^asafaA , (ISd, TA,) or yaA A^asafaA , (Mgh,) from Harabahu “ he despoiled him of his wealth, or property: ” (K:) [or from Hariba , q. v.:] or it originated from the fact that Harb the son of Umeiyeh, when any one died, used to ask his family what they required to expend on the occasion, and used to supply them therewith; (TA;) and when he himself died, the people of Mekkeh and its neighbourhood bewailed him, saying, waA HarobaA , (Th, K, * TA,) or waA HarobaAho , (TA,) [ Alas for Harb! ] and then they changed the expression to waA HarabaA , (Th, K,) or waAHarabaAho , and it became used in the case of bewailing any person who was dear, and in the cases of other calamities: but this account of the origin did not please ISd. (TA.) ― -b2- Also Perdition. destruction, or death. (Har p. 158.)

sourceDefinition: [The male chameleon; ] the male of what is called A^um~u HubayonK ; (S, Msb, K; [but see the latter appellation in art. Hbn ;]) a well-known animal: (TA:) or a certain reptile, like the EaZaA='ap , (K,) said to be larger than this latter, (Msb,) somewhat larger, (S,) that turns itself, (S, Msb,) or its head, (K,) towards the sun, (S, Msb, K,) turning with the sun as the sun turns, and assuming various colours (S, Msb) by reason of the heat of the sun: (S:) Az describes it as a reptile resembling in form what is called saAm~u A^aboraSa , with four legs, slender head, [which is not correct as applied to the chameleon,] and striped back; that all the day looks towards the sun; and he adds that its flesh is impure, and the Arabs never eat it: (TA:) [accord. to Freytag, the word, thus applied, is said (but I know not on what authority) to be from xurobaA , meaning HAfZ Al$ms (guardian of the sun):] the fem. is with p : (S:) and the pl. HaraAbiY~u . (S, Msb.) [The word HrbA' is used in passages cited in the TA as masc. and fem.; whence it seems that it may be written HirobaA='u as well as HirobaA='N .] The Arabs used the expression HirobaA='u tanoDubK or tanoDuba , like *y^obu gaDFA : (S:) [the latter word in each of these cases being the name of a tree:] the former is proverbially applied to a prudent man; because the HrbA' does not quit the first branch but to leap upon the second. (TA.) The phrase AinotaSaba AlEuwdu fiY AlHirobaA='i is used, by inversion, for AntSb AlHrbA'u fY AlEwdi [ The male chameleon stood erect upon the branch ]: for it stands erect upon stones, and upon the roots or trunks of trees, looking towards the sun, and declines as the sun declines. (TA.) ― -b2- Also (tropical:) The back: or its flesh: (K:) or HirobaA='u Almatoni means the flesh along either side of the backbone: (TA:) or this, (TA,) or AlHrbA'u , (K,) the ridge of the backbone: (K, TA:) or HaraAbiY~u Almatoni (S, L, TA) signifies the portions of flesh, (S,) or the flesh, (L, TA,) along either side of the backbone: (S, L, TA:) the sing. is HirobaA='N ; likened to the HrbA' [or male chameleon] of the desert, and therefore tropical: Kr says that the sing. of HaraAbiY~u AlZ~uhuwri is HirobaA='N accord. to rule; showing that it has no known sing. on the authority of hearsay. (L, TA.) -A2- The nails, (S,) or a nail, (K,) of a coat of mail: (S, K:) or the head of a nail in a ring of a coat of mail: (K:) pl. as above. (TA.) -A3- And Rugged ground: (K:) or rugged and hard ground; accord. to Th; but the word commonly known is HizobaA='N , with záy. (TA.) [This meaning has been supposed to be assigned in the K to muHorabiy^apN ; but the TA shows that such is not the case.]

definition: -A2- Also The upper end of a sitting-room, (Msb, and so accord.
sourceDefinition: : see HarobN , in two places. -A2- Also The upper end of a sitting-room, (Msb, and so accord. to an explanation of the pl. maHaAriybu , in the S, on the authority of Fr,) or of a house, or tent, or chamber; (K;) the chief, or most honourable, sitting-place; (AO, L, Msb, K; *) whence, in a trad., kaAna yakorahu AlmaHaAriyba [ he used to dislike the uppermost, or chief, sitting-places in rooms ]: (L:) the place where kings and chiefs and great men sit: (Msb:) a high place: (As, Hr, TA:) a [ chamber of the kind called ] gurofap : (S, Msb, K:) the highest chamber in a house: a chamber to which one ascends by stairs: (Zj, TA:) a king's closet, or private chamber, into which he retires alone, out of the way of the people: (K:) a [ pavilion, or building of the kind called ] qaSor : (As, TA:) the station of the Imám in a mosque: (K:) the miHoraAb [or niche which shows the direction of the kibleh] of a mosque; from the same word as signifying the “ upper end of a sittingroom; ” (Fr, S, Msb;) or, as some say, because the person praying wars with the devil and with himself by causing the attention of his heart: (Msb:) the highest place in a mosque: (Zj, TA:) the kibleh: (L, TA:) a mosque, or place of worship; so in the Kur xix. 12: (S, L:) a place of assembly. (As, TA.) maHaAriybu baniY A_isoraAy^iyla means The places of worship of the Children of Israel, (T, K,) in which they used to assemble for prayer, (T, TA,) or in which they used to sit; (K;) as though they sat therein to consult respecting war. (TA.) [See also ma*obaHN .] ― -b2- I. q. A^ajamapN , (K,) meaning The haunt of a lion. (TA.) ― -b3- The neck of a beast. (Lth, K, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K,) aor , (Msb, K,) inf. n. HasomN , (Mgh, Msb,) He cut it; or cut it off: (S, Msb, K:) he cut it off entirely. (Mgh, Msb.) ― -b2- Hence, Hasomu AlEaroqi : (S:) you say, Hasama AlEiroqa , (K,) inf. n. as above, (TA,) He cut the vein, and then cauterized it to prevent the flow of the blood: (K:) or this is an elliptical expression, originally Hasama dama AlEiroqi , meaning he stopped the flow of blood from the vein by cauterization. (Msb.) And hence, (Mgh,) AiqoTaEuwhu vum~a A@Hosimuwhu , (S, Mgh,) or AiqoTaEuwA yadahu vum~a A@kowuwhaA [Cut ye off his hand, then cauterize it], (S, * Mgh, * TA,) in order that the blood may stop. (S, Mgh, TA.) You say also, Hasamotu Ald~aAb~apa , meaning I cauterized the beast by successive operations. (Bd in lxix. 7.) ― -b3- [Hence, also,] Hasama Ald~aA='a , (K,) inf. n. as above, (TA,) He stopped the disease by a remedy. (K.) And Hasamatohu A^um~uhu Alr~iDaAEa , and Algi*aA='a , His mother stopped his sucking, and his food: (TA:) and Husima riDaAEuhu [His sucking was stopped]; (K;) said of a child. (TA.) And Hasama fulaAnFA Al$~aYo'a , (K,) inf. n. as above, (TA,) He prevented such a one from attaining the thing. (K.) And A^anaA A^aHosimu EalaY fulaAnK AlA^amora I cut off from him the thing, so that he cannot attain aught thereof. (TA.) See also HusuwmN , below. ― -b4- You say also, Hasamahumo , aor , inf. n. HusuwmN , It caused them to pass away, come to an end, cease, perish, or come to nought. (Zj, TA.) See, again, HusuwmN , below. -A2- Hasama fiY AlEamali , (TK,) inf. n. HusuwmN , (Yoo, K,) He strove, laboured, toiled, or exerted himself, and wearied himself, in work. (Yoo, K, TK.)

sourceDefinition: Unluckiness, or inauspiciousness. (S, * K, * TA.) Some explain it thus in the passage here following. (S, * TA.) ― -b2- sax~arahaA Ealayohimo saboEa layaAli wa vamaAniyapa A^ay~aAmK HusuwmFA , in the Kur lxix. 7, means He sent it (the wind) upon them by force, (Jel,) or made it to prevail against them by his power, (Bd,) [seven nights and eight days] consecutively; (T, S, Bd, K, Jel;) an expression taken from the repetition of the act of cauterization, (T, Bd, Jel.) i. e. the act of the ↓ HaAsim ; (Jel;) whence this word ( HAsm ) is applied to anything made consecutive; (T, TA;) and HusuwmN is its pl.: (T, Bd, TA:) or HusuwmN signifies the making consecutive. and, as an epithet, consecutive, and continuous from first to last: (Fr, TA:) or, accord. to some, AlA^ay~aAmu AlHusuwmN means the days that are consecutive with evil especially; and such ISd thinks to be the meaning: (TA:) or All~ayaAliY AlHusuwmu means the nights that cut off good, or prosperity, (↓ taH~simu Alxayora ,) from their people: (S, * K: [and the like is said by Bd in lxix. 7:]) or HusuwmFA in the Kur means causing them to pass away, come to an end, cease, perish, or come to nought: (Zj, T:) or it may be an inf. n., meaning for the purpose of cutting off: or an inf. n. of a verb meant to be understood, as a denotative of state; i. e. ↓ taHosimuhumo HusuwmFA [agreeably with the explanation of Zj]; and this is confirmed by the reading with fet-h [i. e. HasuwmFA , though this is a very rare form of inf. n.]: (Bd:) you say A^ay~aAmN HusuwmN , (K,) in which case the latter word is an inf. n. used as an epithet, meaning cutting off, or preventing, good, or prosperity; (TA;) and A^ay~aAmu HusuwmK , which has a similar meaning. (K, TA.)

definition: A cause, or means, of cutting off, or stopping;
sourceDefinition: A cause, or means, of cutting off, or stopping; (T, K, TA;) syn. maqoTaEapN . (T, TA.) So in the saying, h`*aA maHosamapN lild~aA='i This is a cause, or means, of cutting off, or stopping, the disease. (K, * TA.) And hence, (TA,) Ealayokumo biAlS~awomi faA_in~ahu maHosamapN liloEiroqi wa ma*ohabapN liloA^a$ari , a trad., (T, S, TA,) meaning [Keep ye to fasting, for it is] a cause, or means, of stopping venereal intercourse, [and a cause, or means, of dispelling exultation, or excessive exultation, and resting the mind upon things agreeable with natural desire:] (TA:) or an impediment to venery, and a cause of diminishing the seminal fluid, and of stopping venereal intercourse or passion, &c. (T, TA.)

definition: A child (TA) whose sucking is stopped: (K, TA:) and whose food is stopped.
sourceDefinition: A child (TA) whose sucking is stopped: (K, TA:) and whose food is stopped. (TA.) And A child badly fed. (S, K.) Hence the prov., walogu juraY~K kaAna maHosuwmFA [The lapping of a little puppy that had been badly fed]: said on the occasion of a greedy person's taking much of a thing that he had not been able to obtain, and that he had became able to obtain; or in ordering one to take much when able. (TA. [See Freytag's Arab. Prov. ii. 817; where another reading is given, namely, maHo$uwmFA in the place of maHosuwmFA , as well as the reading here given.])

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (Msb, K,) inf. n. Ha$amN , (Msb,) He was, or became, angry; (Msb, K;) as also ↓ AHt$m : (Msb:) or the latter signifies he became angered. (TA.) ― -b2- And He was, or became, confounded and stupified by shame; or ashamed and confounded or stupified, and remained speechless and motionless. (Msb.) See also 8. -A2- Ha$amahu , aor. , inf. n. Ha$omN ; (Msb;) or Ha$imahu , aor. ; (K;) He angered him; (Msb, K;) as also ↓ AH$mhu , (IAar, S, Msb, K,) and ↓ H$~mhu . (K.) And, accord. to AZ (S) and El-Fárábee, (Msb,) Ha$amahu , (S, Msb, K,) aor. and , (K,) He annoyed him, (S, Msb, K,) and said to him what he disliked, (K,) and angered him; (S, Msb;) namely, a man sitting with him. (S, Msb, K.) An Arab of chaste speech is related to have said, baniY fulaAnK ↓ *`lika mim~aA yuHo$imu , meaning That is of the things that anger the sons of such a one. (S.) ― -b2- Accord. to IAar, (S,) Ha$amahu signifies He caused him to become confounded and stupified by shame; or to become ashamed and confounded or stupified, and to remain speechless and motionless; (S, K;) as also ↓ AH$mhu : (S, Msb, K:) and both signify it caused him to be affected with shame, shyness, or bashfulness; or to shrink; as in the saying, to one shrinking from food, maA Al~a*iY Ha$amaka , or ↓ A^aHo$amaka , What caused thee to be affected with shame, &c.? (TA.) -A3- Ha$ama , aor. , inf. n. Hu$uwmN , He became fat, or in a good condition of body, after leanness. (K.) And Ha$amati Ald~aAb~apu fiY A^aw~ali Alr~abiyEi , (K,) aor. , inf. n. Ha$omN , (TA,) or Hu$uwmN , (TK,) The beast obtained somewhat of the [ herbage called ] rbyE , in the beginning thereof, and became fat, and in good condition, and large in the belly, (K, TA,) and goodly: (TA:) or, as En-Nadr says, Ha$amati Ald~awaAb~u the beasts became in good condition. (S.) ― -b2- maA Ha$ama mino TaEaAminaA He ate not of our food (K, TA) aught. (TA.) ― -b3- maA Ha$ama AlS~ayoda He hit not, or obtained not, or found not, the game, or object of the chase. (K.) -A4- Ha$ama , inf. n. Ha$omN (TA) and Hu$uwmN , (K,) He was, or became, fatigued, tired, or wearied. (K, TA.) The Arabs say, AlHusuwmu yuwrivu AlHu$uwma Labour, or toil, occasions fatigue. (Yoo, TA.)

AHt$m minohu (S, Mgh, K) and Eanohu , (K,) and AHt$mhu , (S, Mgh,) or this last is not allowable except when mino is meant to be understood, (TA,) signify the same; (S, Mgh;) i. e. He was ashamed of it, or abashed at him; or was ashamed to do it, or shy of doing it: (Mgh, K:) or it signifies, (Mgh,) or signifies also, (K,) he shrank from it, or him: (Mgh, K:) or, as some say, thus used it is vulgar; for Hi$omapN , with the Arabs, is only anger: (Mgh:) but IB cites, from Kutheiyir, A_in~iY mataY lamo yakuno EaTaAw^uhumaA EinodiY bimaA qado faEalotu A^aHota$imu as meaning [ Verily I, when the gift of them two in my possession is not for what I have done, ] am ashamed, or abashed: and in a trad. of 'Alee, respecting the thief, occurs the saying, A_in~iY laA^aHota$imu A^ano laA A^adaEa lahu yadFA , meaning Verily I am ashamed not to leave him a hand; and I shrink from it. (K.) -A2- Also He was, or became, master of many Ha$am [or dependents &c.] and servants. (KL.)

definition: A man's special dependents, consisting of his family and slaves [and others ], or his neighbours, who are angry on his account (K, TA) when an event befalls him;
sourceDefinition: A man's special dependents, consisting of his family and slaves [and others ], or his neighbours, who are angry on his account (K, TA) when an event befalls him; (TA;) as also ↓ Hu$omapN ; (Yoo, TA;) in the K, erroneously, Ha$amapN ; (TA;) and A^aHo$aAmN ; (K;) which IAar thinks to be pl. of Ha$amN used in a sing. sense; (TA;) [for] this word is applied to one [ of such persons ] as well as to a pl. number: (K:) you say, h`*aA AlgulaAmu Ha$amN liY [ This young man, or slave, is a dependent of mine ]: (IAar, TA:) or Ha$amN signifies, (ISk, Mgh, Msb,) or signifies also, (K,) a man's relations and household; (ISk, Mgh, Msb, K;) or his servants; (S, Msb;) and those who are angry on his account (ISk, S, Mgh, Msb) when an event befalls him; (Mgh, Msb;) for which reason they are thus called: (S:) or a man's followers; and those on whose account he should be angry: (Ham p. 614:) or the Ha$am of a man are those who are angry on his account; or those on whose account he is angry: (Har p. 164:) accord. to ISk, (Msb,) it is a word having a pl. signification, and having no proper sing.: (Mgh, Msb:) but some say that it has for its pl. A^aHo$aAmN : (Mgh:) and accord. to the K, ↓ Hu$amaA='u [in the CK Ha$omaA' ] signifies neighbours and guests; as though it were pl. of Ha$iymN , like as kuramaA='u is of kariymN : but [perhaps this should be A^aHo$aAmN ; for] we find in the M, h`w^ulaA='i A^aHo$aAmiY , meaning These are my neighbours, and my guests: (TA:) and ↓ Hu$umN , with two dammehs, signifies slaves; (IAar, TA;) or, as some say, followers, whether slaves or free persons. (TA.) -A2- Also An object of desire or quest; syn. TalabapN [in the CK Talabap ]; and so ↓ Hu$uwmN . (K.) You say, huwa Ha$amuhu It is his object of desire or quest. (TK.)

definition: A bag, or receptacle, (A, TA,) in which a man puts his travelling-provisions;
sourceDefinition: A bag, or receptacle, (A, TA,) in which a man puts his travelling-provisions; (TA;) and any other thing that is conveyed behind a man [ on his beast ]: (A [accord. to which this is a proper signification]:) what the rider conveys behind him: (MF [accord. to whom this is a tropical significatiom, from the same word in the last of the senses mentioned below]:) what is borne, of goods or utensils or the like, upon the horse, behind the rider: (Msb [accord. to which, also, this is tropical]:) anything that is bound at the hinder part of the [ camel's saddle called ] raHol or of the [ saddle called ] qatab : (K:) what is put behind the raHol : they used to put the coats of mail behind their riHaAl , in the [receptacles called] EiyaAb , that they might put them on in case of war: (Ham p. 458:) a thing like a baro*aEap , [ a covering for a camel's back, ] of two kinds; namely, that of the [ cloth called ] Hilos , which is hollowed out, so as to admit the upper part of the camel's hump; and that of the [ saddle called ] qatab , which is behind: ISh says that it (the qatab ) is placed upon the hinder part of the camel, beneath the two hinder curved pieces of wood of the qatab : (TA:) a rifaAdap [or kind of pad, or stuffed thing, ] placed at the hinder part of the qatab : (K:) pl. HaqaAy^ibu . (S, A.) You say, malaA^a Haqiybatahu [ He filled his Hqybp ]. (A.) And A^arodafahu xalofahu EalaYAlHaqiybapi He made him to ride behind him on the Hqybp . (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] (tropical:) A thing [ of an ideal kind ] that one takes upon himself, or lays up for the future [ to be rewarded or punished for it ]. (A.) You say, AiHotamala Haqiybapa suwo'K (tropical:) [ He took upon himself a burden of evil: as though he bound it behind him: see 8]. (A, TA.) And Albir~u xayoru HaqiybapK (tropical:) [ Piety is the best thing that one can take upon himself, and lay up for the future to profit thereby]. (A, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also, accord. to the A, which I follow in marking this signification as tropical, but accord. to the Msb and to MF it is the primary signification,] (tropical:) The hinder parts, or posteriors, (A, Msb, MF, TA,) of a woman, (A, Msb,) and of a man: (TA:) pl. as above. (Msb.) So in the phrase nufuju AlHaqiybapi (tropical:) Large, (A,) or prominent, (TA,) in the posteriors. (A, TA.)

HamorN , (TA,) He pared a thong; stripped it of its superficial part: (S, K:) or he (a sewer of leather or of skins) pared a thong by removing its inner superficial part, and then oiled it, previously to sewing with it, so that it became easy [to sew with; app. because this operation makes it to appear of a red, or reddish, colour]. (Yaakoob, S.) ― -b2- And [hence,] He pared, or peeled, anything; divested or stripped it of its superficial part, peel, bark, coat, covering, crust, or the like: and ↓ Hmr~ , inf. n. taHomiyrN , signifies the same in an intensive degree, or as applying to many objects; syn. q$~r . (TA.) ― -b3- Also, (S, K,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (S,) He skinned a sheep [and thus made it to appear red]. (S, K.) ― -b4- He shaved the head [and thus made it to appear red, or of a reddish-brown colour, the common hue of the Arab skin]. (K.) And Hamarati AlmaroA^apu jilodahaA [ The woman removed the hair of her skin ]. (TA.) The term HamorN is [also] used in relation to soft hair, or fur, ( wabar ,) and wool. (TA.) ― -b5- Hamarahu biAlsawoTi He excoriated him ( qa$arahu ) with the whip. (TA.) ― -b6- Hamara AlA^aroD , aor. and inf. n. as above, It (rain) removed the superficial part of of the ground. (TA.) ― -b7- Hamarahu biAll~isaAni (assumed tropical:) He galled him ( qa$arahu ) with the tongue. (TA.) -A2- Hamira , aor. , (Lth, S, K,) inf. n. HamarN , (Lth, S,) He (a horse) suffered indigestion from eating barley: or the odour of his mouth became altered, or stinking, (K, TA,) by reason thereof: (TA:) or he became diseased from eating much barley, (Lth,) or he suffered indigestion from eating barley, (S,) so that his mouth stank: (Lth, S:) and in like manner one says of a domestic animal [of any kind]: part. n. ↓ HamirN . (TA.) -A3- Hamira EalaY~a , (Sh, K, *) aor. and inf. n. as above, (Sh,) He (a man) burned with anger and rage against me. (Sh, K. *) -A4- Hamirati Ald~aAb~apu , (K,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (TA,) [ The horse ] became like on ass in stupidity, dulness, or want of vigour, by reason of fatness. (K.)

sourceDefinition: (incorrectly written, by some physicians and others, ↓ Hum~arN , with teshdeed, MF) and ↓ HawomarN (which is of the dial. of the people of 'Omán, a form disallowed by MF, but his disallowal requires consideration, TA) The tamarindfruit: (K:) it abounds in the Saráh ( Als~araAp ) and in the country of 'Omán, and was seen by AHn in the tract between the two mosques [ of Mekkeh and El-Medeeneh ]: its leaves are like those of the xilaAf called AlbaloxiY~ : AHn says, people cook with it: its tree is large, like the walnut-tree; and its fruit is in the form of pods, like the fruit of the qaraZ . sourceDefinition: [ Redness; ] a well-known colour; (Msb, K;) the colour of that which is termed A^aHomaru : (S, A:) it is in animals, and in garments &c.; and, accord. to IAar, in water [when muddy; for it signifies brownness, and the like: but when relating to complexion, whiteness: see A^aHomaru ]. (TA.) ― -b2- AlHumorapu [ Erysipelas: to this disease the term is evidently applied by Ibn-Seenà, in vol. ii. pp. 63 and 64 of the printed Arabic text of his qAnwn ; and so it is applied by the Arabian physicians in the present day:] a certain disease which attacks human beings, in consequence of which the place thereof becomes red; (ISk, TA;) a certain swelling, of the pestilential kind; (T, K;) differing from phlegmone. (Ibn-Seenà ubi suprà.) ― -b3- *uw HumorapK Sweet: applied to fresh ripe dates. (K.) ― -b4- See also Himir~N .

definition: [ Red: and also brown, or the like: ] a thing of the colour termed HumorapN : (Msb, K:) it is in animals, and in garments &c.
sourceDefinition: [ Red: and also brown, or the like: ] a thing of the colour termed HumorapN : (Msb, K:) it is in animals, and in garments &c.; and, accord. to IAar, in water [when muddy]: and so ↓ yaHomuwrN : (K:) fem. of the former HamoraA='u : (Msb:) pl. HumorN and HumoraAnN : (K:) or when it means dyed with the colour termed HumorapN , the pl. is HumorN (S, Msb) and HumoraAnN ; for you say viyaAbN HumorN and HumoraAnN [ red garments ]: (TA:) but if you apply it as an epithet to a man, [in which case it has other meanings than those explained above, as will be shown in what follows,] the pl. is A^aHaAmiru (S) and HumorN : (TA:) or if it means a thing having the colour termed HumorapN , the pl. is A^aHaAmiru , because, in this case, it is a subst., not an epithet. (Msb.) ↓ A^aHomariY~N also signifies the same as A^aHomaru : (Ham p. 379:) or, as some say, it has an intensive sense. (TA voce karuwbiy~uwna .) It is said in the S, in art. dk , that HamoraAwaAtN is a pl. of HamoraA='u , like as dak~aAwaAtN , is of dak~aA='u ; but it is not so. (IB in that art.) ― -b2- Applied to a camel, Of a colour like that of saffron when a garment is dyed with it so that it stands up by reason of [ the thickness of ] the dye: (TA:) or of an unmixed red colour; (As, S in art. kmt , and TA;) and so the fem. when applied to a she-goat. (TA.) It is said that, of she-camels, the HamoraA=' is the most able to endure the summer midday-heat; and the waroqaA=' , to endure nightjourneying; and that the SahobaA=' is the most notable and the most beautiful to look at: so said Aboo-Nasr En-Na'ámee: and the Arabs say that the best of camels are the Humor and the Suhob . (TA.) [Hence,] Humoru Aln~aEami signifies (assumed tropical:) The high-bred, or excellent, of camels: and is proverbially applied to anything highly prized, precious, valuable, or excellent. (Mgh, Msb.) ― -b3- Applied to a man, (AA, Sh, Az,) White (AA, Sh, Az, K) in complexion; (Az;) because A^aboyaDu might be considered as of evil omen [implying the meaning of leprosy]: (AA, Sh:) or, accord. to Th, because the latter epithet, applied to a man, was only used by the Arabs as signifying “ pure, ” or “ free from faults: ” but they sometimes used this latter epithet in the sense of “ white in complexion, ” applied to a man &c.: (IAth:) fem., in the same sense, HamoraA='u : the dim. of which, ↓ HumayoraA='u , occurs in a trad., applied to 'Áïsheh. (K, * TA.) So, accord. to some, in the trad., buEivotu A_ilaY AlA^aHomari waAlA^asowadi , (TA,) i. e. I have been sent to the white and the black; because these two epithets comprise all mankind: (Az, TA:) [therefore, by the former we should understand the white and the red races; and by the latter, the negroes: but some hold that by the former are meant the foreigners, and] by the latter are meant the Arabs. (TA.) One says also, [when speaking of Arabs and more northern races,] A^ataAniY kul~u A^asowada minohumo waA^aHomara , meaning Every Arab of them, and foreigner, came to me: and one should not say, in this sense, A^aboyaDa . (AA, As, S.) AlHamoraA='u , also, is applied to The foreigners ( AlEajamu ) [ collectively ]; (S, A, K;) because a reddish white is the prevailing hue of their complexion: (S:) or the Persians and Greeks: or those foreigners mostly characterized by whiteness of complexion; as the Greeks and Persians. (TA.) You say, layosa fiY AlHamoraA='i mivoluhu There is not among the foreigners ( AlEajam ) the like of him. (A.) And accord. to some, AlA^aHomaru waAlA^aboyaDu means The Arabs and the foreigners. (TA.) AlHamoraA='u [so in the TA, but correctly A^abonaA='u AlHamoraA='i ,] is an appellation applied to Emancipated slaves: and Aibonu HamoraA='i AlEijaAni , meaning Son of the female slave, is an appellation used in reviling and blaming. (TA.) ― -b4- Also (tropical:) A man having no weapons with him: pl. HumorN (A, K) and HumoraAnN . (K.) ― -b5- AlHusonu A^aHomaru means Beauty is in AlHumorap [app. fairness of complexion; i. e. beauty is fair-complexioned ]: (TA:) or (assumed tropical:) beauty is attended by difficulty; i. e. he who loves beauty must bear difficulty, or distress: (IAth:) or the lover experiences from beauty what is experienced from war. (ISd, K.) ― -b6- AlA^aHomaru A sort of dates: (K:) so called because of their colour. (TA.) ― -b7- AlA^aHomaru waAlA^aboyaDu Gold and silver. (TA.) And AlA^aHomaraAni Flesh-meat and wine; (S, A, K;) said to destroy men: (S:) so in the saying, naHonu mino A^aholi AlA^asowadayoni laA AlA^aHomarayoni We are of the people of dates and water, not of flesh-meat and wine: (A:) or the beverage called nabiy* and flesh-meat. (IAar.) Also Wine and [ garments of the kind called ] buruwd . (Sh.) And Gold and saffron; (Az, ISd, K;) said to destroy women; i. e. the love of ornaments and perfumes destroys them: (Az:) or these are called AlA^aSofaraAni ; (AO, TA;) and milk and water, AlA^aboyaDaAni ; (TA;) and dates and water, AlA^asowadaAni . (A, TA.) And AlA^aHaAmirapu Flesh-meat and wine and [ the perfume called ] Alxaluwq : (S, K:) or gold and flesh-meat and wine; as also AlA^axaADiru : (TA in art. xDr :) or gold and saffron and Alxaluwq . (ISd, TA.) ― -b8- Almawotu AlA^aHomaru (assumed tropical:) Slaughter; (L, K;) because it occasions the flowing of blood: (TA:) and [so in the L, but in the K “ or ”] (tropical:) violent death: (S, A, L, K:) or death in which the sight of the man becomes dim by reason of terror, so that the world appears red and black before his eyes: (A 'Obeyd:) or it may mean (assumed tropical:) recent, fresh, death; from the phrase next following. (As.) ― -b9- waToA^apN HamoraA='u (tropical:) A new, or recent, footstep, or footprint: opposed to dahomaA='u . (As, S, A.) ― -b10- sanapN HamoraA='u (tropical:) A severe year; (S, K;) because it is a mean between the sawodaA=' and the bayoDA=' : or a year of severe drought; because, in such a year, the tracts of the horizon are red: (TA:) when Aljabohapu [the tenth Mansion of the Moon (see manaAzilu Alqamari in art. nzl )] breaks its promise [of bringing rain], the year is such as is thus called. (AHn.) ― -b11- See also HamoraA='u voce HamaAr~apN . ― -b12- jaA='a biganamihi Humora AlkulaY , and, in like manner, suwda AlbuTuwni , (tropical:) He brought his sheep or goats, in a lean, or an emaciated, state. (A, * TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. xabonN (S, Msb, K) and xibaAnN (S, K) and xubaAnN , (S, ISd,) He folded it, namely, a garment, (S, Msb, K,) &c., (S, K,) in its skirt, (Msb,) and sewed it, (S, K,) in order that it might become shorter; (S, Msb, K;) he contracted it [ in its length ], and sewed it; (M, TA;) he raised its (a garment's) skirt, or lower part, and sewed it higher up, in order that it might become contracted and shortened, as is done with the garment of a child; (Lth, TA;) [ he made a tuck in it, to shorten it; ] i. q. vabanahu . (S, K.) ― -b4- yaxobinu Alka*iba (assumed tropical:) He prepares falsehood. definition: , (S, Msb, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K, &c.,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. xajalN , (S, Msb, &c.,) but not xajaAlapN , [though authorized by the KL, in my copy of which I find it thus written (not xijaAlapN as written by Golius),] for this is a vulgar mistake for xajalapN or xajolN , (Mgh, [so in my copy, but correctly ↓ xajalapN (which may be either a simple subst. or an inf. n. of un.) or xajalN ,]) He was, or became, confounded, or perplexed, and unable to see his right course, by reason of shame: (S, O:) or he was, or became, ashamed, and confounded, or perplexed, and unable to see his right course, (T, M, K,) [or, simply, ashamed, (see xajilN ,)] in consequence of a deed that he had done: (T, M, TA:) thus Alxajalu has a more particular signification than AlHayaA='u : (TA:) or it is like AlAisotiHoyaA='u . (Msb.) ― -b2- And He remained silent, (T, K,) or still, (M,) not speaking nor moving. (K.) ― -b3- And He was, or became, in a confused and dubious case, (JK, M, * K, *) so that he knew not how to extricate himself from it. (M, K.) ― -b4- Also, said of a camel, (tropical:) He went in mud, and became like him who is confounded, or perplexed, and unable to see his right course: (JK, * M, K, TA:) or he stuck fast in mire. (T, TA.) ― -b5- And in like manner, (assumed tropical:) He became agitated, or convulsed, or he struggled, or floundered, with his load: (JK:) or xajila biAloHimoli he was oppressed by the load, (K, TA,) so that he was agitated, or convulsed, or he struggled, or floundered, beneath it. (TA.) ― -b6- And, said of a plant, or of herbage, (tropical:) It was, or became, tall, and tangled, or luxuriant, or abundant and dense; (ISd, K, TA;) and so ↓ Axjl said of the kind of trees termed HayoD . (JK, K.) ― -b7- [And, as inf. n. of xajila ,] xajalN also signifies The bearing richness ill; as when, being rich, one exults, or exults greatly or excessively, and behaves insolently and unthankfully: (S, * K:) or the taking a wide, or an ample, range, or being profuse, when rich. (TA.) It is related in a trad. that he [Mohammad] said to the women, A_i*aA juEotun~a wa A_i*aA $abiEotun~a xajilotun~a , (S, * TA,) i. e. When ye are hungry, ye become lowly, humble, or submissive, and cleave to the dust, or earth; (S and TA in art. dqE ;) or ye bear poverty ill: (TA in the present art.;) and when ye are satiated, [ ye bear richness ill; or] ye exult, or exult greatly or excessively, and behave insolently and unthankfully. (S in the present art.) [See also a verse of El-Kumeyt cited in the first paragraph of art. dqE .] ― -b8- And i. q. baramN [The being affected with disgust, loathing, or aversion; the being vexed, grieved, disquieted by grief, &c.] (K, TA. [In the CK, Albaromu is erroneously put for Albaramu .]) ― -b9- And The being remiss in seeking subsistence. (K.) ― -b10- And The being lazy, or indolent: (Az, ISd, K:) from the verb in the sense explained in the second sentence of this paragraph. (TA.) ― -b11- And i. q. [The being bad, corrupt, &c.]. (M, K.) ― -b12- Also, in a shirt, (assumed tropical:) The being much slit, or rent, in the lower parts, or skirts. (Fr, K.)

definition: A thong, (JK, S, K,) plaited, (TA,) thick and strong, like a ring, (JK, K,) which is fastened upon the pastern of a camel, (JK, S, K,) and to which is attached the sariyHap [or thong ] of the naEol...
sourceDefinition: A thong, (JK, S, K,) plaited, (TA,) thick and strong, like a ring, (JK, K,) which is fastened upon the pastern of a camel, (JK, S, K,) and to which is attached the sariyHap [or thong ] of the naEol [or leathern shoe with which the foot is sometimes protected], (S,) or to which are attached the saraAy^iH [or thongs ] of the nEl : (K:) [it is the n. un. of ↓ xadamN : and its pl. is xidaAmN ; as below: in the TA, said to be tropical; but this is pro- bably a mistake: the other significations here following are all tropical:] accord. to AA, [the pl.] xidaAmN signifies shackles, or hobbles; syn. quyuwdN . (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, (S,) (tropical:) i. q. xaloxaAlN [meaning An anklet ]; (JK, S, Mgh, K;) because sometimes made of thongs, with gold and silver affixed thereon: (S:) pl. xidaAmN , (S,) and [coll. gen. n.] ↓ xadamN . (Ham p. 612.) kaA@lomamohuwrapK A_iHodaY xadamatayohaA is a prov. [meaning (assumed tropical:) Like her who has been dowered with one of her two anklets ]. (JK, TA. [See also mahomuwrapN .]) ― -b3- [And hence, (assumed tropical:) A ring of white a little above the hoof of a horse &c.] You say of a horse, lahu xadamataAni mino xilaAfK , meaning (assumed tropical:) He has a whiteness [or rather a ring of white a little above the hoof ] in his fore leg [or right fore leg ] and another in his left fore leg [probably a mistake of a copyist for his left kind leg ]. (TA in art. xlf .) [The coll. gen. n. ↓ xadamN is used in the Deewán of the Hudhalees, as stated by Freytag, in the sense of (assumed tropical:) A place where the colour differs, like an anklet, on the foot: and a whiteness on the foot of a bull, surrounding it like a circle: and xidaAmN as meaning whiteness: or, as some say, streaks (“striæ”). See also xudomapN .] ― -b4- [Hence, also,] (assumed tropical:) The place where each foot comes forth from the trousers. (TA.) ― -b5- Also (assumed tropical:) The shank; (K;) because it is the place of the xadamap , i. e. the anklet: (TA:) pl. xidaAmN and [coll. gen. n.] ↓ xadamN . (K.) Hence, in a trad. of Selmán, kaAna EalaY HimaArK waEalayohi saraAwiylu waxadamatAhu tu*abo*ibaAni [ He was upon an ass, and upon him were trousers, and his shanks were dangling ]: or, as some say, the meaning here is, the parts from which his two feet came forth, of the trousers. (TA.) And one says, A^abodati AlHarobu Eano xidaAmi Almuxad~araAti (tropical:) [ The war made apparent the shanks, or the anklets, of the girls that had been kept behind the curtains ]; meaning the war became vehement. (A, TA.) ― -b6- Also (assumed tropical:) A ring of people; (S, K;) a compact ring thereof: likened to the thong described in the first sentence of this paragraph. (TA.) Hence the saying of Khálid Ibn-El-Weleed, in a letter that he wrote to the Satraps of Persia, (TA,) AlHamodu lil~`hi Al~a*iY faD~a xadamatakumo , meaning [ Praise be to God, ] who hath dispersed, or broken up, your congregation: (S, * K, * TA:) for when the thong above mentioned is broken, or parted, the saraAy^iH [or thongs of the leathern shoe] become loosed, and the shoe falls off: so says IAth, and A'Obeyd says the like. (TA.)

(TA.) ― -b2- Hence, (S,) (tropical:) i. q. xaloxaAlN [meaning An anklet ]; (JK, S, Mgh, K;) because sometimes made of thongs, with gold and silver affixed thereon: (S:) pl. xidaAmN , (S,) and [coll. gen. n.] ↓ xadamN . [See also mahomuwrapN .]) ― -b3- [And hence, (assumed tropical:) A ring of white a little above the hoof of a horse &c.] You say of a horse, lahu xadamataAni mino xilaAfK , meaning (assumed tropical:) He has a whiteness [or rather a ring of white a little above the hoof ] in his fore leg [or right fore leg ] and another in his left fore leg [probably a mistake of a copyist for his left kind leg ]. (TA in art. xlf .) [The coll. gen. n. ↓ xadamN is used in the Deewán of the Hudhalees, as stated by Freytag, in the sense of (assumed tropical:) A place where the colour differs, like an anklet, on the foot: and a whiteness on the foot of a bull, surrounding it like a circle: and xidaAmN as meaning whiteness: or, as some say, streaks (“striæ”). See also xudomapN .] ― -b4- [Hence, also,] (assumed tropical:) The place where each foot comes forth from the trousers. (TA.) ― -b5- Also (assumed tropical:) The shank; (K;) because it is the place of the xadamap , i. e. the anklet: (TA:) pl. xidaAmN and [coll. gen. n.] ↓ xadamN . (K.) Hence, in a trad. of Selmán, kaAna EalaY HimaArK waEalayohi saraAwiylu waxadamatAhu tu*abo*ibaAni [ He was upon an ass, and upon him were trousers, and his shanks were dangling ]: or, as some say, the meaning here is, the parts from which his two feet came forth, of the trousers. (TA.) And one says, A^abodati AlHarobu Eano xidaAmi Almuxad~araAti (tropical:) [ The war made apparent the shanks, or the anklets, of the girls that had been kept behind the curtains ]; meaning the war became vehement. (A, TA.) ― -b6- Also (assumed tropical:) A ring of people; (S, K;) a compact ring thereof: likened to the thong described in the first sentence of this paragraph. (TA.) Hence the saying of Khálid Ibn-El-Weleed, in a letter that he wrote to the Satraps of Persia, (TA,) AlHamodu lil~`hi Al~a*iY faD~a xadamatakumo , meaning [ Praise be to God, ] who hath dispersed, or broken up, your congregation: (S, * K, * TA:) for when the thong above mentioned is broken, or parted, the saraAy^iH [or thongs of the leathern shoe] become loosed, and the shoe falls off: so says IAth, and A'Obeyd says the like. (TA.)
