definition: A she-camel not having having her fore shank and her arm bound together: (TA:) or not having upon her a xiTaAm [or halter ]: (IDrd, O, K:) or repairing to the water;
sourceDefinition: A she-camel not having having her fore shank and her arm bound together: (TA:) or not having upon her a xiTaAm [or halter ]: (IDrd, O, K:) or repairing to the water; and so ↓ miTolaAqN ; (Aboo-Nasr, K, TA;) of which latter she pl. is maTaAliyqu : (TA:) or that is left a day and a night and then milked: (K:) pl. TawaAliqu and A^aTolaAqN and TalaqapN ; which last is expl. by AA as meaning she-camels that are milked in the place of pasturing. (TA.) See also TuluqN , first sentence: and for an explanation of the pl. TawaAliqu applied to camels, see TalaqN , second sentence. Also (O), TaAliqN , (S, O,) or TaAliqapN , (K,) signifies A she-camel which the pastor leaves for himself, not milking her at the water: (S, O, K:) the former is expl. by Esh-Sheybánee as meaning one which the pastor leaves [ with her udder bound ] with her SiraAr , not milking her in the place where she lies down to rest: (TA:) or the latter signifies, (Lth, O, K,) and the former also, (Lth, O,) a she-camel that is set loose among the tribe to pasture where she will in any part of the tract adjacent to their place of alighting or abode, (Lth, O, K, [ mn jinAnihimo in the CK being erroneously put for mino janaAbihimo ,]) that has not her fore shank and her arm bound together when she returns in the afternoon or evening, nor is turned away [ from the others ] in the place of pasturage: (Lth, O:) or TaAliqN signifies a she-camel, (S, Msb,) and a ewe, (S,) that is set loose, or dismissed, to pasture where she will: (S, Msb:) and also as first expl. in this sentence: (S:) it is mentioned by ElFárábee as signifying a ewe left to pasture by herself, alone. (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence,] TaAliqN and TaAliqapN , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) the former, without p , used by all, (Msb,) the latter occurring in a verse of El-Aashà, (S, Mgh, * O, Msb,) ending a hemistich, and pronounced TaAliqapN , (S, O, Msb, [which cite the verse somewhat differently,]) (tropical:) A woman [ divorced, or] left to go her way, (S, * Mgh, * O, Msb, *) or separated from her husband [ by a sentence of divorce ]: (S, * Mgh, * Mgh, * K, TA:) both mentioned by Akh: (O, TA:) accord. to IAmb, one says TaAliqN only, because it applies only to a female: accord. to Lth and IF, TaAliqapN means TaAliqapN gadFA [ divorced, &c., to-morrow ]; and Lth adds that it is thus to accord with its verb, Talaqato : some, however, say that the h is affixed in the verse of El-Aashà by poetic license, to complete the hemistich; but an Arab of the desert, in reciting this verse to As, is related to have said TaAliqN [which equally completes the hemistich]: and the Basrees hold that the sign of the fem. gender is elided in TaAliqN because it is a possessive epithet, meaning *aAtu TalaAqK [ having divorce ]. (Msb.) ― -b3- A^uwojuhN TawaAliqu : ― -b4- and layolapN TaAliqapN and layaAlK TawaAliqu : see TaloqN , latter half.

sourceDefinition: (S, M, Msb, K, &c.) and ZirobaAnN (AA, AZ, Msb, TA) and ZarobaAnN (IJ, TA) and ↓ ZirabaA='u (M, CK, TA, or ↓ ZirobaA=' or ↓ ZiribaA=' accord. to two different copies of the K) A small, stinking beast, (AZ, S, M, Msb, K,) resembling a cat, (AZ, S, M, K,) or resembling a short Chinese dog, (Msb,) or resembling an ape or a monkey, (AA, T, M, TA,) or above the whelp of a dog, (El-Mustaksee, TA,) that often emits a noiseless wind from the anus; (M, Msb, * TA;) said by Az, on the authority of the handwriting of AHeyth, to be a beast that has small legs, their length being that of half a finger, but which is broad, its breadth being equal to the space measured by the extension of the thumb and the little finger, or of the thumb and the fore finger, and its length being a cubit, having a compact head, and its ears [for AdnAh , in my original, I read A^u*unaAhu ] being like the cat's; (TA;) it is small and short in the ears, ( A^aSolamu AlA^u*unayoni , M, Msb,) or having a stoppage of the ears, ( A^aSam~u AlA*nyn , TA,) its earholes [ only ] hearing a confused, or humming, or ringing, sound; (M, TA;) long in the snout, [but El-Farezdak speaks of it as having a short nose, as is shown in the S,] black in the back, white in the belly; (M, Msb, TA;) it is said that its back is [ or rather contains ] one single bone, without any qafaS [or cage-formed structure of ribs, &c. ], and that the sword has no effect upon it by reason of the hardness of its skin, unless striking its nose: (TA:) the pl. is ZaraAbiynu , (M, K,) or ZaraAbiY~u , (AZ, T, S, Msb,) sometimes, (S,) or this latter also, (M, K,) as though it were pl. of ZirobaA=' , (S,) or the first Y is a substitute for the A [of the sing. ZaribaAnN ] and the second for the n , (M,) and (quasi-pl. ns., M, K) ↓ ZirobaY (AZ, T, M, Msb, K) and ↓ ZirobaA='u , (M, K,) or ↓ ZirobaY , is a pl. like HijolaY pl. of HajalN , (S, TA,) and these two are [said to be] the only pls. of this measure, (AHei, TA,) and Lth and AHeyth say that ZirobaA='u is incorrect, and is rightly ↓ ZirobaY . (T, TA.) A poet says, (namely, 'Abd-Allah Ibn-Hajjáj Ez-Zebeedee, M, TA,) A^alaA A^aboligaA qayosFA waxinodifa A^an~aniY Darabotu kaviyrFA maDoriba AlZ~aribaAni [ Now tell ye Keys and Khindif that I have struck Ketheer in the place of striking of the ZrbAn ], meaning that he had struck Ketheer Ibn-Shiháb (S, M, TA) El-Medh-hijee upon his face; for the ZrbAn has a line, or long mark, upon his face; and he likens the blow that he inflicted upon his face to that mark: [see maDoribN :] and the same words of the latter hemistich, except that EubayodFA is substituted in them for kaviyrFA , occur in a verse of Asad Ibn-Nághisah, who slew 'Obeyd by order of En-Noamán. (TA.) One says, fasaA bayonanaA AlZ~aribaAnu , (S,) or bayonahum , (Msb, K,) [lit. The ZrbAn emitted a noiseless wind from its anus among us, or among them, ] a prov., (S,) meaning that we, or they, became disunited, and alienated, one from another: [for] when this animal emits a noiseless wind from its anus in the garment of a man, the stink does not go away until the garment wears out: (S, Msb, K:) the Arabs of the desert assert that it does so in the garment of him who hunts it: (S:) and it is said to do so in the hole of the [lizard called] Dab~ , which, being stupified by the foulness of the stink, is taken and eaten by it. (M, K, TA.) One says also, ta$aAtamaA fakaA^an~amaA jazaraA bayonahumaA ZaribaAnFA [ They reviled each other, and it was as though they slaughtered between them a ZrbAn ]: the foulness of their reviling being likened to the stink of that animal. (M, TA.) And yatanaAzaEaAni jiloda AlZ~aribaAni They two contend in pulling at the skin of the ZrbAn , meaning (assumed tropical:) they revile each other: (M, TA:) and yatamaA$anaAni jiloda AlZ~aribaAni They wipe their hands together upon the skin of the ZrbAn , [likewise] meaning (assumed tropical:) they revile each other. (IAar, T, TA.)

sourceDefinition: [accord. to some] signifies Four teeth behind the nawaAji* [or other grinders; app. meaning, of a horse ]: (K:) or the sockets ( A^asonaAx ) of the teeth: (S, K:) [and it is said that] A^aZoraAbu All~ijaAmi signifies the knots that are at the extremities of the bit. (M, TA.) J cites the following verse, ascribing it to 'Ámir Ibn-Et-Tufeyl, wamuqaT~iEK Halaqa Alr~iHaAlapi saAbiHK baAdK nawaAji*uhu Eani AlA^aZoraAbi [thus in the S, (but in the M and TA EalaY AlA^aZoraAbi ,) as though meaning And breaking in pieces the rings of the girth of the saddle, running with the fore legs well stretched forth, his grinders appearing from the sockets ]: but IB says, [following the reading in the M and TA,] the verse is by Lebeed; and the poet is describing a horse that breaks in pieces the rings of the saddle by his springing forward, and whose grinders ( nawaAji*uhu ) appear when he treads upon the [stones, or hills, called] ZiraAb : [see ZaribN , of which both ZiraAbN and A^aZoraAbN are said to be pls.:] also that the right reading is wamuqaT~iEN [and saAbiHN ]: and by the nwAj* are meant the DawaAHik [or teeth next behind the canine teeth], accord. to Hr. (TA.)

definition: The eighteenth letter of the alphabet: called EayonN .
sourceDefinition: The eighteenth letter of the alphabet: called EayonN . It is [one of the letters termed majohuwrap , or vocal, i. e. pronounced with the voice, not with the breath only; and] of the letters termed Haloqiy~ap [or faucial]; these being E and H and h and x and g [and A^ ]; the lowest of which in its place of utterance is E ; wherefore Kh [in the composition of his lexicon entitled “ Kitáb el-'Eyn ”] and several other lexicographers [after him] began their books with [words having] this letter [in their roots], giving the next place to H , the next to h , the next to x , and the next to g . (L, TA.) It is substituted for ' [in what is termed the EanoEanap of Temeem]; as in Eano for A^ano : and for H ; as in Eat~aY for Hat~aY , and SuboEN for SuboHN : and for g ; as in EulaAmN for gulaAmN . (MF, TA.) It is never consociated with H in any word of which the letters are all radicals; unless it be a word compounded of two words, as HayoEala from HaY~a EalaY . (Kh, TA.) -A2- [As a numeral, it denotes Seventy. ]

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. EibaAdapN (IKtt, L, Msb, &c.) and EubuwdapN and Eubuwdiy~apN (IKtt) and maEobadN and maEobadapN , (L,) He served, worshipped, or adored, God; rendered to Him religious service, worship, or adoration: (L:) or he obeyed God: (IKtt:) or he obeyed God with humility or submissiveness; rendered to Him humble, or submissive, obedience: (IAth, L, Msb:) [or, inf. n. EibaAdapN , he did what God approved: and, inf. n. EubuwdapN , he approved what God did: (see the former of these ns. below:)] the verb is used in these senses only when the object is God, or a false god, or the Devil. (TA.) -A2- Eabadotu bihi A^uw*iyhi I was excited against him to annoy, molest, harm, or hurt, him. (O, K.) ― -b2- And maA Eabadaka Ean~iY What has withheld thee from me? (IAar, L.) -A3- Eabuda , aor. , inf. n. EubuwdapN and Eubuwdiy~apN , accord. to Lh and IKtt, but A'Obeyd held that there is no verb to these two ns., He was, or became, a slave, or in a state of slavery: or he was, or became, in a state of slavery, his fathers having been so before him; as also ↓ Eub~ida . (L.) ― -b2- Lth read [in the Kur v. 65] waEabuda AlT~aAguwtu ; explaining the meaning to be, Et-Tághoot having become an object of worship; and saying that Eabuda , here, is a verb similar to Zarufa and faquha : but Az says that in this he has committed a mistake. (L.) -A4- Eabida , aor. , inf. n. EabadN (and EabadapN , or this is a simple subst., L), He was, or became, angry; (Fr, S, O, * L, Msb, K;) [and so ↓ tEb~d , in the Deewán of Jereer, accord. to Freytag;] like A^abida and A^amida and A^aHina : (Fr:) and he was long angry. (L.) You say, Eabida Ealayohi He was angry with him. (Fr.) And ElFarezdak makes it trans. without a prep., saying yaEobaduniY . (L.) ― -b2- He disdained, or scorned. (AZ, S, O, L.) El-Farezdak says, waA^aEobadu A^ano A^ahojuw kulayobFA bidaArimi [ And I disdain to satirize Kuleyb with Dárim: the former being unworthy to be coupled with the latter even as an object of satire]. (S, O, L.) [See also EabidN .] ― -b3- He denied, disacknowledged, or disallowed. (O, K.) [See, again, EabidN .] ― -b4- He repented, and blamed himself, (O, K, TA,) for having been remiss, or having fallen short of doing what he ought to have done. (TA.) ― -b5- He mourned, grieved, or was sorrowful. (L.) ― -b6- He was covetous; or inordinately, or culpably, desirous. (O, K.) And Eabida bihi He clave, or kept, to it, or him, inseparably. (L.) ― -b7- And, (O, L, K,) said of a camel, (L,) He was, or became, affected with mange, or scab: (L:) or with incurable mange or scab: (O, L:) or with severe mange or scab. (K.)

definition: , originally an epithet, but used as a subst.
sourceDefinition: , originally an epithet, but used as a subst., (Sb, TA,) A male slave; (S, A, O, L, Msb, K;) i. q. mamoluwkN ; (L, K;) [but EabodN is now generally applied to a male black slave; and mamoluwkN , to a male white slave; and this distinction has long obtained;] contr. of Hur~N ; (S, A, O, L, Msb;) as also ↓ EabodalN , (L, K,) in which the l is augmentative: (L:) and a servant, or worshipper, of God, and of a false god, or of the Devil: (Lth, L, &c.:) [you say Eabodu A@ll~`hi and Eabodu Al$~amosi &c.: see also EaAbidN , which signifies the same; and see the remarks in this paragraph on the pls. EabiydN and EibaAdN and EabadapN &c.:] and a man, or human being; (M, A, L, K;) as being a bondman ( marobuwbN ) to his Creator; (L;) applied to a male and to a female; (Ibn-Hazm, TA;) whether free or a slave: (K:) pl. A^aEobudN (S, O, Msb, K) and A^aEobidapN and A^aEobaAdN , (IKtt, TA,) [all pls. of pauc.,] of which the first is the most commonly known, (Msb,) and ↓ EabiydN and EibaAdN , (S, O, Msb, K,) which two and the first are the most commonly known of all the many pls. of EabodN , (Msb,) EabiydN being like kaliybN as pl. of kalobN , a rare form of pl.; (S, O;) or, accord. to some, it is a quasipl. n.; accord. to Ibn-Málik, faEiylN occurs as a pl. measure, but sometimes they use it in the manner of a pl. and make it fem., as in the instance of EabiydN , and sometimes they use it in the manner of quasi-pl. ns. and make it masc., as in the instances of HajiyjN and kaliybN ; (MF;) [accord. to the general and more approved opinion, it is a quasi-pl. n., and therefore fem. and masc., but most commonly fem.;] and further it should be remarked that the common people agree in making a difference between EabiydN and EibaAdN , by the former meaning slaves [and by the latter meaning servants of God and also simply, with the article Al , mankind ], saying, h`w^ulaA='i EabiydN these are slaves, and h`*aA EabodN mino EibaAdi A@ll~`hi [ this is a servant, of the servants of God ]: (Az, L:) [and a distinction is also made between EibaAdN and EabadapN , respecting which see what follows:] other pls. of EabodN are EubodaAnN , (S, O, K,) like tumoraAnN pl. of tamorN , (S, O,) and EibodaAnN , (S, O, K,) like jiHo$aAnN pl. of jaHo$N , (S, O,) and EubudN , (S, O, K,) like suqufN pl. of saqofN , (S, O,) or this is pl. of EabiydN , like rugufN pl. of ragiyfN , (Zj,) and is also a pl. of EaAbidN , (L,) and some read [in the Kur v. 65] Eubuda AlT~aAguwti , (Akh, S, O,) and EubodN (MF) and EubuwdN and Eub~adN and Eub~aAdN and EabadapN , (IKtt, TA,) the last three of which are also pls. of EaAbidN : (L:) one says of the worshippers of a plurality of gods, humo Eabadapu AlT~aAguwti [ they are the servants of Et-Tághoot ]; but the Muslims one calls EibaAdu A@ll~`hi , meaning the servants, or worshippers, of God: (Lth, L:) [all these are pls. in the proper sense of the term, of the broken class:] and Eaboduwna , (O, K,) a pl. of the sound class, adopted because EabodN is originally an epithet: (TA:) and [the following, with the exception of the first, and of some which are particularized as being pls. of pls., are also said to be pls., but are properly speaking quasi-pl. ns., namely,] ↓ EabudN , (O, K,) accord. to some, who read [in the Kur ubi suprà] Eabuda AlT~aAguwti , making the former a prefixed noun, as meaning the servants ( xadam ) of Et-Tághoot; but it is a n. of the measure faEulN , like Ha*urN and nadusN , not a pl.; the meaning being the servant ( xaAdim ) of Et- Tághoot; (Akh, S, O;) and it is also used by poetic license for EabodN ; (Fr, T, S, O;) and ↓ Eibid~aAnN and ↓ Eibid~aA='u and ↓ Eibid~aY ; (S, O, K;) or, accord. to some, the last of these signifies slaves born in a state of slavery; and the female is termed ↓ EabodapN ; and Lth says that ↓ Eibid~aY signifies a number of slaves born in a state of slavery, generation after generation; but Az says that this is a mistake, that Eibid~aY A@ll~`hi signifies the same as EbaAdu A@ll~`hi , that it is thus used in a trad., and that Eibid~aY is applied in another trad. to poor men of the class called A^aholu AlS~uf~ap ; (L;) and ↓ Eubud~aA='u and ↓ Eibid~apN and ↓ EibaAd~N (IKtt, TA) and ↓ maEobadapN , like ma$oyaxapN , (T, O, K,) and ↓ maEobuwdaA='u (Yaakoob, S, O, K) and ↓ maEobuwdaY , (IKtt, TA,) and [pl. pl.] ↓ maEaAbidu , (O, K,) said to be pl. of maEobadapN ; (TA;) and pl. pl. A^aEaAbidu , (K,) pl. of A^aEobudN ; (TA;) and Eabiyduwna , (Es-Suyootee, MF,) app. pl. of ↓ EabiydN . (MF.) faA@doxuliY fiY EibaAdiY , in the Kur lxxxix. 29, means Then enter thou among my righteous servants: (Ksh, Bd, Jel:) or it means fiY HizobiY [ among my peculiar party ]. (S, O.) ― -b2- Also (tropical:) Ignoble, or base-born; like as Hur~N is used to signify “ generous, ” “ noble, ” or “ well-born. ” (Mgh in art. Hr .) -A2- Also A certain plant, of sweet odour, (O, K, TA,) of which the camels are fond because it makes the milk to become plentiful, and fattens; it is sharp, or hot, ( HaAd~ O, or HaAr~ TA,) in temperament; and when they depasture it they become thirsty, and seek the water: (O, TA:) so says IAar. (O.) -A3- And A short and broad naSol [or arrow-head, or spear-head, or blade ]. (AA, O, * K.)

sourceDefinition: and ↓ EaAbidN (but the latter is rarely used, Ibn-'Arafeh) Angry. (L.) And (both words) Disdaining, or disdainful; scorning, or scornful. (L.) Accord. to AA, AlEaAbidiyna in the words of the Kur [xliii. 81], A_ino kaAna lilr~aHom`ni waladN faA^anaA A^aw~alu ↓ AlEaAbidiyna , means The disdainers, or scorners, and the angry: (S, * L:) but Ibn-'Arafeh rejects this assertion: (TA:) these words are variously explained; as meaning There is not to the Compassionate a son; and I am the first of the angry disdainers or scorners of the assertion that there is: or, and I am the first of the deniers of this assertion: or, and I am the first of the worshippers of God according to the unitarian doctrine, or, of the worshippers of God of this people: or if there were to the Compassionate a son, I would be the first of his worshippers: or if there be to the Compassionate a son, I am the first of worshippers; but I am not the first worshipper of God: or, accord. to Az, the best interpretation is one ascribed to Mujáhid; i. e. if there be to the Compassionate a son in your opinion, I am the first of those who have worshipped God alone, and who have thus charged you with uttering a falsehood in this your assertion. (L.)

sourceDefinition: and Eabodal~aAwiY~N [both post-classical, the latter, which is the more common, said by Forskål to be an appellation of the Cucumis chate, which is app. from qiv~aA=' , denoting several species of cucumber; but it is] a sort of melon, [ abounding in Egypt, of little flavour, eaten with sugar, ] said to be thus called in relation to 'AbdAllah Ibn-Táhir, a governor of Egypt on the part of El-Ma-moon. sourceDefinition: and EabaAbiydu , each a pl. having no sing., Parties of people (S, O, K) going in every direction: (S, O:) and horsemen going in every direction. (K.) One says, SaAra Alqawomu EabaAdiyda and EabaAbiyda The people became divided into parties going in every direction. (S, O.) (TA.) ― -b2- Also (both words, K, or the latter [only], TA,) Far-extending roads: (K:) or diverse and far-extending roads: said to be used in this sense not with respect to coming, but only with respect to dispersion, and going away. (K, TA.) ― -b4- And one says, mar~a raAkibFA EabaAdiydahu He passed, or went away, riding upon the extremities of his buttocks. (O, K.)

sourceDefinition: , applied to a camel, Rendered submissive, or tractable; broken, or trained; syn. mu*al~alN : (A, L:) or anointed with tar, (S, O, K,) and rendered submissive, or tractable: (S, O:) or whose whole skin is anointed with tar: (Sh:) or mangy, or scabby, whose fur has fallen off by degrees, and which is set apart from the other camels to be anointed with tar: or rendered submissive by the mange, or scab: or affected with the mange, or scab; or with incurable mange or scab. (L. [And, applied to a camel, it has other meanings, which see in what follows.]) [And hence, app.,] safiynapN muEab~adapN A ship, or boat, tarred: (AO, S, O, L, K:) or smeared with fat, or oil. (AO, L.) ― -b2- Applied to a road, Beaten; syn. mu*al~alN ; (S, A, O, K;) trodden; (Az, TA;) or travelled by many passengers going to and fro: (TA:) and syn. with mu*al~alN as applied to other things also. (K.) ― -b3- And [hence] A wooden pin, peg, or stake. (Az, O, K, TA. [In the CK, Almuw^at~adu is erroneously put for Alwatidu .]) So in the following verse of Ibn-Mukbil: waDam~anotu A^arosaAna AljiyaAdi muEab~adFA A_i*aA maA DarabonaA raA^osahu laA yuran~aHu [ And I made a wooden peg to be a guarantee for the ropes of the coursers: when we beat its head, it did not wabble ]. (Az, O, TA.) ― -b4- Also Honoured, or treated with honour, (L, K,) and served; applied to a camel. (L.) Thus it has two contr. significations. (K.) ― -b5- And A camel left unridden. (O, L.) ― -b6- And, applied to a stallion [camel], Excited by lust, or by vehement lust. (O, K.) ― -b7- Also, applied to a country, or tract of land, In which is no footprint, or track, nor any sign of the way, nor water: (O, K:) you say baladN muEab~adN . (O.)

definition: , (S, O,) inf. n. taEoriybN , (S,) He (an Arab) arabicized a foreign word; spoke it, or pronounced it, agreeably with the ways of Arabic speech; (S;) as also ↓ AErb , (S, O, *) inf. n. A_iEoraAbN ....
sourceDefinition: , (S, O,) inf. n. taEoriybN , (S,) He (an Arab) arabicized a foreign word; spoke it, or pronounced it, agreeably with the ways of Arabic speech; (S;) as also ↓ AErb , (S, O, *) inf. n. A_iEoraAbN . (TA.) ― -b2- And He taught another the Arabic language. (TA, from a trad.) ― -b3- See also 4, in fourteen places. ― -b4- The inf. n. signifies also The showing, or declaring, one's saying, (K, TA,) and one's deed, (TA,) to be bad, evil, abominable, or foul. (K, TA.) One says, Er~b Ealayohi He showed him, or declared to him, that his saying, and his deed, was bad, &c.; and upbraided him for it. (TA.) And faEalotu ka*aA waka*aA famaA Ear~aba EalaY~a A^aHadN I did so and so, and no one upbraided me; or charged me with having acted disgracefully. (AZ, TA.) And Er~b Ealayohi fiEolahu , (S, O,) and qawolahu , (TA,) He showed him, or declared to him, that his deed was bad, evil, abominable, or foul, (S, O,) and so his saying. (TA.) taEoriybN is The saying to a man who has uttered what is foul, or erroneous, “ It is not so, but so; ” telling him what is more correct. (Sh, TA.) And The replaying against a speaker; (K, TA;) and so ↓ A_iEoraAbN . (TA.) One says, Er~b Ealayohi He replied against him, denying or disallowing or disapproving what he said: (S:) or he prevented, hindered, or forbade, him: or he did so, and denied or disallowed or disapproved [ what he said or did ]. (TA.) [See what next follows.] ― -b5- Also The treating medically, to remove his disease, one whose stomach is in a corrupt, or disordered, state. (O, K. [In both, Alt~aEoriybu is expl. as meaning tamoriyDu AlEaribi i. e. Al*~aribi AlmaEidapi . Freytag has strangely rendered the verb as signifying “ ægrotum reddidit aliquem stomachi corruptio. ”]) Az says that Alt~aEoriybu followed by EalaY and having for its object him who says what is disapproved may be from this. (TA.) ― -b6- Also The lopping a palm-tree; or pruning it by cutting off some of its branches. (S, O, K. *) ― -b7- And The scarifying a horse or similar beast in the parts of the skin next the hoofs and then cauterizing those parts: (K, TA:) or the cauterizing a horse in several places in those parts, and then gently scarifying them without producing any effect upon the sinews, or tendons, (Az, O, TA,) in order to strengthen the parts, (Az, TA,) or in order that the hair may become strong: (O:) or Er~b Alfarasa signifies he made an incision in the bottom of the horse's hoof; and the verb implies that, by this operation, what was concealed becomes apparent to the eye, so that one knows the state of the hoof, whether it be hard or soft, sound or diseased. (L, TA. See also 1 in art. bzg .) -A2- Also, the inf. n., The getting, or procuring for oneself, an Arabian horse. (TA. [See also 4, near the end.]) ― -b2- And The taking, or making, for oneself, an Arabian bow. (O, K.) -A3- Also the drinking much clear, or limpid, water, (O, K,) which is termed Earib . (O.) -A4- Er~b Albaqarapa , (K,) or ↓ A^aEorabahaA , (O,) He rendered the cow desirous [ of copulation ]; said of a bull. (O, K.) -A5- And Er~b , (Fr, Mgh, O,) inf. n. taEoriybN ; (Fr, O, K;) and ↓ AErb , (Fr, Mgh, O, Msb,) inf. n. A_iEoraAbN ; (Fr, Mgh, K;) and ↓ Earobana ; (O, and S and K in art. Erbn ;) He gave what is termed an Eurobuwn (O, Msb, K) or EurobaAn (Fr, Mgh) [i. e. an earnest ], fiY ka*aA [ in the case of such a thing ], (O,) or fiY bayoEihi [ in the case of his purchase ]. (Msb.) One says, ↓ A^aEorabuwA fiY Ald~aAri A^arobaEamiAy^apK They paid in advance, as an earnest, in the case of the house, four hundred [dirhems]. (L, TA.) It is related in a trad. that ↓ AlA_iEoraAb in buying and selling is forbidden: (Mgh, O, TA:) this is said by Sh to mean A man's saying to another, If I do not purchase this for so much, thou shalt have such and such of my property. (O, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (AZ, Msb, TA,) [for AErb AlkalaAma , like AfSH for AfSH AlkalaAma ,] inf. n. A_iEoraAbN , (A, K,) He spoke clearly, plainly, distinctly, or intel-ligibly, (AZ, A, Msb, K, * TA,) in Arabic; (Msb;) as also ↓ tEr~b , and ↓ AstErb ; said of a foreigner, or one [previously] not clear, plain, distinct, or intelligible, in speech: (AZ, Msb, TA:) and ↓ Earuba , aor. , inf. n. EurobN and EuruwbN , accord. to Th, and EurobapN and EiraAbapN [which accord. to general analogy would be EaraAbapN ] and Euruwbiy~apN ; (TA;) or ↓ Eariba , aor. ; (Msb;) [likewise] signifies he spoke clearly, plainly, or distinctly, after being barbarous, or vitious, in speech: (Msb, TA:) and ↓ Earuba he spoke without incorrectness; (Msb;) and [so AErb , for] A_iEoraAbN signifies the committing no error in speech: (K, TA:) and the expressing of meanings clearly, plainly, distinctly, or perspicuously, by words. (TA.) [↓ Er~b , also, has a similar meaning:] it is said in a trad., A^ano ↓ kaAnuwA yasotaHib~uwna A^ano yulaq~inuwA AlS~abiY~a Hiyna yuEar~ibu yaquwla laA A_ilaAha A_il~aA A@ll~`hu saboEa mar~aAtK (O, TA) i. e. [ They used to like teaching the boy, ] when he spoke distinctly, or articulately, [ to say “ There is no deity but God ” seven times. ] (TA.) And one says, AErb AlkalaAma , and AErb bihi , meaning He made the speech [that he spoke] clear, plain, distinct, or perspicuous. (TA.) And AErb biHuj~atihi He declared, or spoke out clearly or plainly, his argument, plea, allegation, or the like, without fearing any one. (S, O.) And A^aEorabotu Al$~aYo'a and AErbt Eanohu , and ↓ Ear~abotuhu and Er~bt Eanohu , which last, accord. to Fr, is better than Er~bthu and AErbthu , I made the thing clear, plain, distinct, or manifest. (Msb.) And AErb Eam~aA fiY Damiyrihi He declared, or spoke out clearly or plainly, what was in his mind. (TA.) And AErb Eanohu lisaAnuhu , and ↓ Er~b Enh , His tongue made clear, or plain, or spoke clearly, or plainly, for him: and Eam~aA fiY ↓ yuEar~ibu qalobihi lisaAnuhu His tongue tells plainly, or declares, what is in his heart. (Az, TA.) It is said in a trad., Alv~ay~ibu tuEoribu Eano nafosihaA , (S,) or AlA^ay~imu , and ↓ tuEar~ibu , accord. to different relaters, but some say the former only, (Msb,) i. e. [ She who has become a widow, or been divorced, &c., or she who has no husband, whether she be a virgin or not, or not being a virgin, ] shall speak out plainly for herself [when demanded in marriage]: (S, Msb:) or Alv~ay~ibu yuEoribu EanohaA lisaAnuhaA , so accord. to IKt, (O,) or EnhA ↓ yuEar~ibu , (Mgh, O,) so accord. to A 'Obeyd, but, as IAmb says, both are dial. vars. of which neither is preferable to the other; and the meaning is [ she who has become a widow, &c., her tongue ] shall declare for her. (O.) One says also, AErb Eani Alr~ajuli He spoke out, or explained, for the man. (TA.) And Eani Alqawomi ↓ Ear~abotu I spoke for the people, or party; (Fr, S, Mgh, * O, K;) and pleaded for them; (Fr, Mgh, * TA;) as also A^aEorabotu ; but the former in this sense is better known. (Mgh.) And AErb Eanohu , and Enh ↓ Er~b , He pleaded his cause. (TA.) And Eano HaAjatihi ↓ Er~b He spoke and pleaded for the object of his want. (A.) ― -b2- AErb also signifies He was, or became, chaste, uncorrupt, or free from barbarousness, in speech; although not an Arab. (Msb.) And lahu AlkalaAma ↓ Ear~abotu , inf. n. taEoriybN ; as also A^aEorabotu lh , inf. n. A_iEoraAbN ; I made the speech [that I spoke] clear, or plain, to him, so that there was in it no barbarousness. definition: He assimilated himself to the Arabs.
sourceDefinition: He assimilated himself to the Arabs. (S.) He (a man not of genuine Arabian descent) introduced himself among the Arabs, and spoke their language, and imitated their manner or appearance; [ he became a naturalized, or an insitious, Arab; (see AlEarabu ;)] as also ↓ AstErb . (Az, TA.) ― -b2- He became an Arab of the desert; (S, Mgh;) he returned to the desert, (Az, Mgh, TA,) after he had been dwelling in a region of cities or towns or villages and of cultivated land, and joined himself to the Arabs of the desert. (Az, TA.) Hence, tEr~b baEoda hijoratihi He became an Arab of the desert [ after his flight, or emigration, for the sake of El-Islám], (S, Mgh,) returning to the desert. (Mgh.) ― -b3- He dwelt, or abode, in the desert. (O, K.) ― -b4- See also 4, first sentence. ― -b5- taEar~abato lizawojihaA She acted in an amorous manner, or with amorous dalliance, and mani- fested love, to her husband. (A, TA.) ― -b6- Respecting a meaning assigned to tEr~b by Golius and Freytag, see 4, latter half.

sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K, &c.,) as also ↓ AlEurobu , (S, O, Msb, K,) A certain people, or nation; [ the Arabs, or Arabians; ] (S, O;) the contr. of AlEajamu (A, Msb, K, TA) and AlEujomu ; (TA;) the inhabitants of the cities, or large towns, (S, A, O, K,) or of the Arabian cities and towns or villages: (Mgh:) [but now, on the contrary, generally applied to those who dwell in the desert:] or those who have alighted and made their abode in the cultivated regions, and have taken as their homes the Arabian cities and towns or villages, and others also that are related to them: (Az, Msb:) or [accord. to general usage] an appellation of common application [ to the whole nation ]: (T, K:) [and in the lexicons and lexicological works applied to the desert Arabs of pure speech: ] it is of the fem. gender: (Msb, K:) and AlEarabu has two pls., namely, AlEurubu , with two dammehs, and AlA^aEorubu [which is a pl. of pauc.]: (Msb:) the rel. n. [which serves as a sing.] is ↓ EarabiY~N : (S, O, K: [ EarabN EarabiY~N in the CK is a mistake:]) accord. to Az, (TA,) this appellation is applied to a man of established Arab lineage, even if he be not chaste, or correct, in speech. (Msb, TA.) The dim. of AlEarabu is ↓ AlEurayobu , (S, O,) without p , (O, TA,) an extr. word [with respect to analogy, as the undiminished noun is fem.]: (TA:) a poet (Abu-l-Hindee, whose name was 'Abd-El-Mu-min, son of 'AbdEl-Kuddoos, O, TA) says, wamakonu AlD~ibaAbi TaEaAmu AlEurayobi walaA ta$otahiyhi nufuwsu AlEajamo [ And the eggs of dabbs are food of the little Arabs; but the souls of the Foreigners do not desire them ]: in which he uses the dim. form to imply respect, or honour, like as it is used in the saying A^anaA ju*ayoluhaA AlmuHak~aku waEu*ayoquhaA Almuraj~abu [expl. in art. j*l ]. (S, O.) ― -b2- ↓ AlEarabu AlEaAribapu (in which the latter word is used as a corroborative of the former as in layolN laAy^ilN , S, O) and ↓ AlEarabu AlEarobaA='u (S, A, O, Msb, K) and ↓ AlEarabu AlEarabiy~apu (O) and ↓ AlEarabu AlEaribapu (K) and ↓ AlEarabu AlEaribaAtu (CK [but this I do not find in any other copy of the K]) are appellations of The pure, or genuine Arabs: (S, A, O, K:) or those who spoke the language of Yaarub Ibn-Kahtán; which is the ancient language: (Msb:) and ↓ AlEarabu AlmusotaEoribapu , (S, O, Msb, K,) as also ↓ AlEarabu AlmutaEar~ibapu , (S, O, K,) is an appellation of The insititious [or naturalized Arabs ]; (K;) those who are not pure, or genuine, Arabs: (S, O:) or those who spoke the language of Ismá'eel [or Ishmael ] the son of Ibráheem [or Abraham ], i. e., the dialects of El-Hijáz and the parts adjacent thereto: (Msb:) and the appellation of ↓ musotaEoribapN is thought by Az to apply [also] to people not of pure Arabian descent, who have introduced themselves among the Arabs, and speak their language, and imitate their manner or appearance. (TA.) [The former division is most reasonably considered as consisting of the extinct tribes ('Ád, Thamood, and others mentioned in what follows); or of these together with the unmixed descendants of Kahtán, whose claims to the appellation of genuine Arabs are held by many to be equally valid: and the latter division, as consisting of those whose origin is referred, through Ma'add and 'Adnán, to Ismá'eel (or Ishmael), whose wife was descended from Kahtán. What I find in the TA, on this subject, is as follows.] The former of these two divisions consisted of nine tribes, descendants of Irem [or Aram] the son of Sám [or Shem] the son of Nooh [or Noah]; namely, 'Ád, Thamood, Umeiyim, 'Abeel, Tasm, Jedees, 'Imleek [or Amalek], Jurhum, and Webári; and from them Ismá'eel [or Ishmael is said to have] learned the Arabic language: and the ↓ mutaEar~ibap are [said to be] the descendants of Ismá'eel, the descendants of Ma'add the son of 'Adnán the son of Udd: so says Abu-l-Khattáb Ibn-Dihyeh, surnamed Dhun-Nesebeyn: or the former division consisted of seven tribes, namely, 'Ád, Thamood, 'Imleek, Tasm, Jedees, Umeiyim, and Jásim; the main portion of whom has become extinct, some remains of them, only, being scattered among the [existing] tribes: so says IDrd: and the appellation of ↓ AlEarabu AlEaAribapu is also given to the descendants of Yaarub the son of Kahtán [only]. (TA.) [It should be observed, however, that the appellation of ↓ AlmutaEar~ibapu is, by those who hold the extinct tribes above mentioned as the only genuine Arabs, applied to the unmixed descendants of Kahtán; and ↓ AlmusotaEoribapu , to those who are held to be the descendants of Ismá'eel: thus in the Mz, 1st nwE . Also, it should be observed that the appellation of ↓ AlEarabu AlEaAribipu , in the conventional language of Arabic lexicology, is often applied to the Arabs of the classical ages, and the later Arabs of the desert who retained the pure language of their ancestors, indiscriminately: it is thus applied by writers quoted in the Mz (1st nwE ) to all the descendants of Kahtán, and those of Ma'add the son of 'Adnán (through whom all the descendants of Ismá'eel trace their ancestry) who lived before the corruption, among them, of the Arabic language.] ― -b3- ↓ AlA^aEoraAbu is the appellation given to Those [ Arabs ] who dwell in the desert; (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K;) such as go about in search of herbage and water; and Az adds, whether of the Arabs or of their freedmen: he says that it is applied to those who alight and abide in the desert, and are neighbours of the dwellers in the desert, and journey, or migrate, with them, to seek after herbage and water: (Msb:) it is not a pl. of AlEarabu , not being like AlA^anobaATu , which is pl. of Aln~abaTu ; (S, O;) but is a [coll.] gen. n.: (S:) AlA^aEaAriybu occurs as its pl. sourceDefinition: and EurobuwnN and ↓ EurobaAnN (Mgh, * O, Msb, K) and ↓ Eurub~aAnN , mentioned on the authority of Ibn-Es-Seed, as of the dial. of El-Hijáz, and EarobuwnN , mentioned by AHei, but this last is a vulgar word, and is disallowed by Lb; (TA;) as also A^arabuwnN and A^urobuwnN and A^urobaAnN ; (Mgh, * Msb, K;) [ An earnest, or earnest-money; ] a portion of the price, whereby a bargain is ratified; (K, TA;) a thing that is paid by the purchaser of a commodity, (Mgh, O, Msb,) or by the hirer of a thing, (Msb,) on the condition that if the sale (Mgh, O, Msb) or hire (Msb) have effect, it shall be reckoned as part of the price, and otherwise shall not be reclaimed; (Mgh, O, Msb;) called by the vulgar rabuwn : (O:) it is forbidden in a trad., (Mgh, O, TA,) and by most of the lawyers, but allowed by some: (TA:) Erbwn is said by As to be a foreign word arabicized, (Msb,) and so say many authors; though it is said by some of the expositors of the Fs to be from Alt~aEoriybu signifying “ the making clear, plain, ” &c.; Arbwn being also derived from A^urobapN signifying “ a knot: ” (TA:) and [it is said that] the n in Erbwn and ErbAn may be augmentative or radical, because one says A^aEoraba fiY ka*aA and Earobana . definition: A woman who manifests love to her husband;
sourceDefinition: A woman who manifests love to her husband; (IAar, S, O, K, TA;) and is obedient to him; (IAar, TA;) as also ↓ EaruwbapN : (TA:) and (so in the O and TA, but in the CK “ or ”) a woman disobedient to her husband; (IAar, O, K, TA;) unfaithful to him by unchastity; corrupt in her mind: (IAar, O, TA:) as though having two contr. meanings; [the latter meaning] from Earob [a mistranscription for Earab ] signifying “ corruptness ” of the stomach: (O:) or who loves him passionately, or excessively: or who manifests love to him, evincing passionate, or excessive, desire: [lit., evincing that; meaning what is expressed by the words immediately preceding it; for otherwise this last explanation would be the same as the first; and as I have rendered it, it is nearly the same as an explanation in the Expos. of the Jel (lvi. 36), manifesting love to her husband, by reason of passionate, or excessive, desire: ] (K:) and (so in the TA, but in the CK “ or ”) a woman who is a great laugher: and ↓ EaruwbapN and ↓ EaribapN signify the same: (K:) the pl. of the first is EurubN (S, O, K) and EurobN ; (TA;) and the pl. of ↓ EaribapN is EaribaAtN : (K:) IAth says that ↓ EaribapN signifies a woman who is eager for play, or sport: and EurubN , he adds, is pl. of ↓ EariybN , which signifies a woman of goodly person, who manifests love to her husband: and it is also said that EurubN signifies women who use amorous gesture or behaviour, and coquettish boldness, with feigned coyness or opposition: or who make a show of, or act with, lasciviousness: or passionately loving: and ↓ EaribapN and EaruwbN , accord. to Lh, signify a woman passionately loving, and lascivious. (TA.)

definition: [ Safflower, or bastard saffron;
sourceDefinition: [ Safflower, or bastard saffron; i. e., cnicus, or carthamus tinctorius; ] a certain dye, (S, O,) or plant, (Msb, K,) well known, (O, Msb,) with which one dyes, (M,) the first juice ( sulaAfap ) of which is called jiroyaAl , (TA,) and one of the properties of which is that it causes tough meat to become thoroughly cooked, so as to fall off from the bone, (K, * TA,) when somewhat thereof is thrown into it: (TA:) its seed is called quroTumN : (K:) there are two kinds of it; one of the cultivated land, and one of the desert; and both grow in the country of the Arabs: (M, TA:) it is an Arabicized word. (Az, TA.)

EaSaAfiyru . (Msb.) Accord. to Hamzeh, it is so called because it was disobedient, and fled, EaSaY wafar~a . (MF, TA.) [This, I believe, is said to have been the case when the beasts and birds &c. were summoned before Adam, to be named by him. See the Kur ii. 29-31.] ― -b2- [It is also applied to Any passerine bird. (TA.) ― -b5- naq~ato EaSaAfiyru baTonihi [lit. The sparrows of his belly cried ], (K,) like naq~ato DafaAdiEu biTonihi , alluding to the intestines, is also a prov., (TA,) meaning (tropical:) he was, or became, hungry. (K, TA.) In like manner also one says, laA taA^okulo Hat~aY taTiyra EaSaAfiyru baTonika , meaning (tropical:) Eat thou not until thou be hungry. (TA.) -A2- A^aSaAfiyru Almuno*iri is an appellation of (assumed tropical:) Certain excellent camels, that belonged to kings: (S, O, K:) or certain excellent camels that belonged to En-Noamán Ibn-El-Mundhir were called A^aSaAfiyru Aln~uEomaAni . (T, TA.) -A3- AlEuSofuwru also signifies The male locust. (O, K.) -A4- And The chief, or lord. (IAar, O, K.) ― -b2- And The king. (K.) -A5- Also A portion, (S, O,) or small portion, (K,) of the brain, (S, O, K,) beneath the farox of the brain, (TA,) as though separated therefrom: (S, O, TA:) between the two is a pellicle. (S, O, K.) ― -b2- And A certain vein in the heart. (IF, O.) ― -b3- And A prominent bone in the temple of the horse, (S, O, K,) on the right and on the left; both being called EuSofuwraAni . (S, O.) ― -b4- And The place whence grows the forelock [app. of the horse ]. (M, K.) ― -b5- And A narrow blaze extending downwards from the blaze on the forehead of the horse, not reaching to the muzzle. (O, K.) ― -b6- The EaSaAfiyr of a camel's hump see expl. voce EuroSuwfN . -A6- And EuSofuwrN signifies also A piece of wood in the [ kind of camel-vehicle called ] hawodaj , uniting the extremities of certain [ other ] pieces of wood therein; [perhaps what unites the outer extremities of two long pieces of wood which project horizontally from the lower part of the hwdj , from the two extremities of either side;] (K;) having the form of the [ kind of saddle called ] A_ikaAf : (L:) or the pieces of wood which are in the [ kind of camel's saddle called ] raHol , by which the heads of the [ curved pieces of wood called the ] A^aHonaA=' are fastened [ together ]: (K:) and the wood by which are fastened the heads of the [ kind of saddle called ] qatab : (K:) the pl. is EaSaAfiyru : or the ESAfyr of the qtb are its EaraASiyf , from which ESAfyr is formed by transposition; and they are four pins of wood which are put between [or rather which unite or conjoin ] the heads of the AHnA=' of the qtb ; in each Hinow are two of these pins, fastened with sinews or with camel's skin; and in it [or appertaining to the same part ] are the ZalifaAt : (S, O:) or the nails which unite the head of the qtb : (IDrd:) or the EuSofuwr of the [kind of saddle called] A_ikaAf is its EuroSuwf , from which latter word the former is formed by transposition; and it is a piece of wood fastened between [or rather uniting or conjoining ] the anterior HinowaAni . (S, O.) In a trad. it is said that it it is unlawful to cut or shake off aught from the trees of El-Medeeneh, except for the ESfwr of a qtb , or to supply a sheave of a pulley, or for the handle of an iron implement. (S.) ― -b2- Also A nail of a ship. (O, K.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (S, O, Msb, K,) inf. n. EaDodN , (Msb,) He hit, or hurt, his EaDud [or upper arm, between the elbow and the shoulder-blade ]; (S, O, Msb, K;) i. e., a man's. (Msb.) ― -b2- And, aor. as above, (S, A, &c.,) and so the inf. n., (Msb,) (tropical:) He aided, or assisted, him; (S, A, O, Msb, K;) he was, or became, an EaDud i. e. aider, or assistant, to him: (Msb:) thus used, it is doubly tropical; for EaDudN primarily [and properly] relates to the arm, then it was metaphorically applied to signify an aider, or assistant, then they formed the verb in this meaning, and it obtained so extensively as to become a Haqiyqap Eurofiy~ap [i. e. a word so much used in this tropical sense as to be, in the said sense, conventionally regarded as proper]; therefore it is not mentioned by Z [in the A] as tropical; (TA;) and ↓ EADdhu , (K, * TA,) inf. n. muEaADadapN , (S, A, O, TA,) likewise signifies he aided him against another. (S, * K, * TA.) ― -b3- Also, EaDadahu , He (a camel) took him (another camel) by his EaDud [i. e. arm ], and threw him down. (L.) ― -b4- EaDadahu fiY AlEaDudi [ He bound it, or attached it, upon the EDd (or upper arm )]; namely, a thong, or the like; (O, K, TA;) such, for instance, as an amulet. (TA.) ― -b5- EaDada Ald~aAb~apa , aor. , [thus I find it in this instance,] inf. n. EuDuwdN [in the TA EDd ,] He walked by the side [as though by the EaDud (or arm )] of the beast, (L, Msb,) on the right or left, (Msb,) or sometimes on its right and sometimes on its left, not quitting it. (L.) ― -b6- EaDada Alr~akaAy^iba , (L, K,) aor. , inf. n. EaDodN , (L,) He came to the camels, or other beasts, used for riding, from the tracts, or parts, surrounding them, and gathered them together. (L, K. *) ― -b7- See also 4. ― -b8- EaDada Al$~ajara , aor. , (S, Mgh, O, &c.,) inf. n. EaDodN , (Mgh, Msb,) (tropical:) He cut, or lopped, the trees (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K *) with a miEoDad ; (S;) as also ↓ AstEDdhu . (Hr, O, K. *) ― -b9- And EaDada Al$~ajarapa (tropical:) He scattered the leaves from the tree for his camels. (Th, TA.) ― -b10- EaDadahu Alqatabu , (O, K,) inf. n. EaDodN , (TA,) The saddle galled and wounded him; namely, a camel. (O, K.) -A2- EuDida , (L, K,) a verb like EuniYa , (K,) He had a complaint of his EaDud [or upper arm ]. (L, K.) And in like manner are formed verbs relating to all other members, or parts of the body. (L.) -A3- EaDida He (a camel) had the disease termed EaDadN [q. v.]. (S, O, K.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, O, Msb, K,) which is the most common form of the word, (TA,) and ↓ EaDidN , (S, O, Msb, K,) of the dial. of Asad, (O, Msb,) and ↓ EuDudN , (AZ, O, Msb, K,) of the dial. of Tihámeh, (AZ, TA,) or of El-Hijáz, (Msb,) and ↓ EaDadN , (Th, TA,) and ↓ EaDodN , (S, O, Msb, K,) of the dials. of Temeem and Bekr, (O, Msb,) and ↓ EuDodN , (S, O, Msb, K,) and ↓ EiDodN , (K,) the last three of which are said to be contractions of the first or second, or variants thereof formed to assimilate them to other words preceding them; (TA;) all masc. and fem.; (L;) or fem. only; (Lh, TA;) or masc. in the dial. of Tihámeh; (AZ, L;) or fem. in the dial. of Tihámeh, and masc. in the dial. of Temeem; (AZ, Msb;) i. q. saAEidN , (S, L,) i. e. [The upper arm, or upper half of the arm, ] from the elbow to the shoulder-blade, (S,) or the part between the elbow and the shoulderblade, (L, O, Msb, K,) of a human being: (L:) [and in a beast, the arm; (see A^abaDahu &c.;) in this case like *iraAEN :] pl. A^aEoDudN and A^aEoDaAdN , (Msb,) or only the latter, (L,) which is used in a poem of Sá'ideh Ibn-Ju-eiyeh as meaning the legs of bees. (TA.) malaA^a mino $aHomK EaDudiY , in the story of Umm-Zara, means (assumed tropical:) He filled with fat, not peculiarly my EaDud , but my whole body; for when the EaDud becomes fat, the whole body becomes so. (O, L.) ― -b2- [Hence,] EaDudN [in the CK AlEaDodu is erroneously put for AlEaDudu ] signifies also (tropical:) An aider, or assistant; (L, K, TA;) and so [app. any of its variants mentioned above, and] ↓ EaADidN (TA) and ↓ EiDaAdapN . (L, TA.) And it is also used for [its pl.] A^aEoDaAdN ; as in the Kur xviii. 49, in which the sing. form is said to be employed for the sake of agreement with the other verses [preceding and following], that they may all end with singulars: (TA:) but one also says, humo EaDudiY and A^aEoDaAdiY (tropical:) [ They are my aiders, or assistants ]. (O, K, TA.) And one says, fulaAnN EaDudiY , meaning (assumed tropical:) Such a one is my support, or stay. (Msb.) And fat~a fiY EaDudihi (assumed tropical:) He broke some of the intentions, purposes, or designs, of his aiders, or assistants, (or of the people of his house, TA,) and separated, or dispersed, them from him: (O, K:) or he sought to injure him by diminishing, or impairing, [ in number or power, ] the people of his house; (T and O in art. ft ;) and in like manner, fat~a fiY A^aEoDaAdihi . (TA in the present art.) And fat~a fiY EaDudiY wahad~a rukoniY (assumed tropical:) He broke my strength, and dispersed, or separated, my aiders, or assistants: (TA in art. ft :) [for] EaDudN signifies also (tropical:) Strength, because the part so called, of a man, is a mean of strength to him. (L.) sana$ud~u EaDudaka biA^axiyka , in the Kur [xxviii. 35], means, accord. to Zj, (tropical:) We will aid thee, or assist thee, by thy brother. (L.) ― -b3- Also (assumed tropical:) The side of the armpit; and so ↓ EaDadN . (L.) And (assumed tropical:) A side of a road; (O, L; [in this sense written in the TA EaDodN ;]) as also ↓ EiDaAdapN . (L.) (assumed tropical:) The side, or quarter, from which the wind blows. (L.) (assumed tropical:) A side; or a lateral, or an outward, or adjacent, part, or portion; a quarter region, or tract; (O, L, K;) of a house, and of anything: pl. A^aEoDaAdN . (L.) [Hence,] EaDudu Alr~akaAy^ibi (assumed tropical:) The tract, or part, surrounding the camels, or other beasts, used for riding. (L.) One says, Aimoliko A^aEoDaAda AlA_ibili (tropical:) [lit. Have thou possession of the tracts adjacent to the camels ], meaning direct thou aright the course of the camels, so that they may not wander away to the right and left. (A.) ― -b4- Also, and ↓ EaDadN , (L,) and A^aEoDaAdN , (S, L, K,) which last is a pl. of the two preceding words, as is also EuDuwdN , (L,) (tropical:) A raised enclosing border, or such borders, of built work, (S, O, L, K,) &c., (S, L,) of a watering-trough or tank, and of a road, &c., (K,) or of anything, (S, O,) such as the A^aEoDaAd of a watering-trough or tank, which are stones, (S,) or broad and thin stones, (L,) set up around the brink; (S, L;) also called EaDudN ; extending from the place whence the water flows into it, to its hinder part: (L:) or EaDudN signifies the two sides of a watering-trough or tank: (IAar, L:) or its side: (O, TA:) and its A^aEoDaAd are its sides: and the A^aEoDaAd of a portion of sown land that is separated from the parts adjacent to it by ridges of earth, for irrigation, are its raised borders that confine the water; (A;) A^aEoDaAdu AlmazaAriEi signifying the [ raised ] boundaries between the portions of sown land. (En-Nadr, L.) ― -b5- EaDudN (O, K, in the CK EaDod ,) is also syn. with ↓ EaDiydN , (K,) or ↓ EaDiydapN , (O,) as signifying (assumed tropical:) A row of palm-trees: (O, K:) the first of these words is mentioned by Hr as occurring in a trad., and is thus expl.: but others say that it is ↓ EaDiydN , (TA,) which, accord. to As, signifies a palm-tree having such a [ low ] trunk that one can reach from it [ the fruit or branches ]; (S, TA;) and the pl. is EiDodaAnN : (S, K:) he adds that when it exceeds the reach of the hand it is called jab~aArapN . (S, TA.) ― -b6- EaDudaA Aln~aEoli and ↓ EiDaAdataAhaA [and EaDudaA $iraAki Aln~aEoli signifies (assumed tropical:) The two branches of the $iraAk of the sandal, described voce A^u*unN , q. v.;] the two appertenances, of the sandal, that lie upon the foot. (L.) ― -b7- EaDudaA Alr~aHoli (assumed tropical:) The two pieces of wood that are attached to the fore part of the camel's saddle, (L,) or to the lower portions of its fore part (the waAsiT ): (Lth, O, L:) or, accord. to AZ, the upper portions of the ZalifataAni [a mistake for the HinowaAni ] of the camel's saddle, next [ the pieces of wood called ] the EaraAqiY ; below them being the ZalifataAni , which are the lower parts of the HinowaAni of the waAsiT and of the muw^ax~arap . (O, L. [See ZalifapN . In a similar manner, also, the term EaDudaAni is used in relation to a horse's saddle: see qarabuwsN .]) ― -b8- See also EaDaAdN .

definition: Having a complaint of his EaDud [or upper arm ].
sourceDefinition: Having a complaint of his EaDud [or upper arm ]. (O, K.) ― -b2- A camel having the disease termed EaDadN . (TA.) ― -b3- One that has drawn near, or approached, to the EaDudaAni [i. e. the two sides ] (O, TA) of the watering-trough, or tank. (O, K.) ― -b4- A male [wild] ass that has drawn together the she-asses ( AlA^utuna ) from their several quarters ( mino jawaAnibihaA ); as also ↓ EaADidN : (O, K:) the former occurs in a verse of El-Akhtal, describing a sportsman shooting at [wild] asses. (O.) ― -b5- yadN EaDidapN An arm of which the EaDud [or portion between the elbow and the shoulder-blade ] is short. (ISk, S, O, K.) And EaDudN EaDidapN A short upper arm. (TA.) -A2- See also EaDudN , first sentence. ― -b2- And see EaDaAdN .

definition: and EaDaAdK A woman thick and ugly in the EaDud [or upper arm ]: (Fr, O, * K:) or, as some say, short.
sourceDefinition: and EaDaAdK A woman thick and ugly in the EaDud [or upper arm ]: (Fr, O, * K:) or, as some say, short. (TA.) And the former, applied to a man and to a woman, signifies Short: (O, K:) or this epithet is applied to a woman, and ↓ EaDudN and ↓ EaDidN and ↓ EaDodN are applied in this sense to a man. (L.) And EaDaAdK , [in the CK and my MS. copy of the K EaDaAdN , but it is] like rabaAEK , applied to a boy, or young man, Short, compact, of moderate dimensions, (O, K, TA,) firm in make. (TA.) ― -b2- naAqapN EaDaAdN A she-camel that does not come to the watering-trough, or tank, to drink, until it is left to her unoccupied; that cuts herself off from the other camels: (O, L:) such is also termed qa*uwrN . (L.)

definition: [a word of a very rare measure (see yaEoqiydN )] A certain herb, or leguminous plant;
sourceDefinition: [a word of a very rare measure (see yaEoqiydN )] A certain herb, or leguminous plant; (S, O, K;) also called Taraxo$aquwqN , (S, O, TA, [and hence supposed by Golius to be the taraxicon, with which the description has little agreement,] in the T taraxojaquwq , TA,) this being an Arabicized word from [the Pers.] talox kuwk : accord. to Aboo-Ziyád, it is a herb, or leguminous plant, of those termed A^aHoraAr , bitter, and having a yellow blossom, desired by the camels and the sheep or goats, and liked also by the horses, which thrive upon it; and it has a viscous milk: (O:) it is a herb, or leguminous plant, of which the blossom is more intensely yellow than the waros [q. v.]: or, as some say, it is of the class of trees ( mina Al$~ajari [but this term $jr is often applied to small plants]): and some say that it is of the herbs, or leguminous plants, of [ the season called ] the rabiyE , having in it a bitterness: thus in the M. (TA.)

definition: Anything thick, big, or coarse;
sourceDefinition: Anything thick, big, or coarse; (S, O, * K;) as also EulunodFY : (O, K:) and bulky, strong, and tall; applied to a camel and to a horse: (TA:) and sometimes they applied the epithet EulunodFY to a camel: (S:) this and ↓ EulaAdFY signify strong, so applied, (O, K,) as does also ↓ EalnodadN applied to a horse; (L;) or bulky and tall, applied to a camel and to a horse: or, accord. to En-Nadr, one says naAqapN EalanodaApN , meaning a great and tall she-camel; but not jamalN EalanodFY ; like as one says naAqapN EafaronaApN ; but not jamalN EafaronFY : (TA:) and ElndY occurs in old poetry as an epithet applied to a she-camel [app. in this instance with what is termed the fem. alif, i. e. without teshdeed]: (Ham p. 82:) the pl. of EalanodFY is EalaAnidu (S, O) and EalaAdaY : and Sb mentions [app. as a dial. var. of the sing.] ↓ EaladonFY . (L.) ― -b2- Also A species of tree, (O, K, TA, and so in a copy of the S,) of the kind called EiDaAh , having thorns: (O, K:) [a coll. gen. n.:] n. un. EalanodaApN ; (AHn, O, K: *) it is of the trees of the sands, not such as is termed HamoD , (O, TA,) and yields an intense smoke: (TA:) accord. to Lth, the ElndAp is a tall tree, having no thorns, of the kind termed EiDaAh : but he is incorrect in so saying: it is a tree having hard branches, for which the cattle, or camels and other beasts, have no desire, and not of the kind termed EiDaAh ; and indeed how can it be of the kind thus termed having no thorns? nor is it tall, the tallest being of the height of a man sitting; but, with its shortness, it is dense and compact in its branches. (Az, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, O, Msb, K,) inf. n. taEomiyrN ; (S, Msb;) and ↓ Eamarahu , (Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb,) inf. n. EamorN ; (TA;) God lengthened, or prolonged, his life; (S, O, Msb, TA;) made him to continue in life; preserved him alive; (K, TA;) as also ↓ AstEmrhu . (O and Bd in xi. 64.) It is said in the Kur [xxxv. 12], wamaA yuEam~aru mino muEam~arK walaA yunoqaSu A_il~aA fiY kitaAbK , i. e., No one whose life is prolonged has life prolonged, nor is aught diminished of his, meaning another's, life, but it is recorded in a writing: (I'Ab, Fr, * O: *) or the meaning is, nor does aught pass of his, i. e. the same person's, life: (Sa'eed Ibn-Jubeyr:) both these explanations are good; but the former seems more probably correct. (Az, TA.) ― -b2- Em~r nafosahu He determined for himself, or assigned to himself, a limited life. (K.) ― -b3- Em~r A@ll~`ha , inf. n. taEomiyrN , He acknowledged the everlasting existence of God. (S, TA.) ― -b4- Eam~arotuka A@ll~`ha I ask, or beg, God to prolong thy life: (Ks, O, TA:) or I remind thee of God. (TA, app. on the authority of Mbr.) [It also seems to signify I swear to thee by the everlasting existence of God. See Eamora A@ll~`hi .] ― -b5- A^uEam~iruka A@ll~`hua A^ano tafoEala ka*aA I adjure thee by God, and beg thee by the length of thy life, that thou do such a thing. (K, * TA.) ― -b6- See also 4. -A2- Eam~ara xibaA='F bimaA A@HotaAja A_ilayohi [ He furnished a tent with what he required ]. (Msb in art. bnY .)

definition: and ↓ EumorN are both inf.
sourceDefinition: and ↓ EumorN are both inf. ns., signifying the same. (S, O.) [See 1. As such, the former is the more common.] And both of these words, (Mgh, K, &c.,) and ↓ EumurN , (K, &c.,) [used as simple substs., or abstract ns., in which case the second is more common than the first, except in forms of swearing, in which the former is used, and the third is more chaste than the second,] signify Life; (Msb, K;) [the age to which the life extends; ] the period during which the body is inhabited by life: so that it denotes less than baqaA='N : wherefore the latter is [frequently] used as an attribute of God; but Emr is seldom used as such: (Er-Rághib, B:) pl. A^aEomaArN . (K.) You say ↓ A^aTaAla A@ll~`hu Eumuraka and Eamoraka [ May God prolong thy life ]. (S, O.) In a form of swearing, Eamor only is used. (S.) [In a case of this kind, when l is not prefixed to it, it is in the accus. case, as will be shown and expl. below: but when l is prefixed to it, it is in the nom.] You say laEamoruka laA^afoEalan~a , meaning By thy life, I will assuredly do [such a thing]. (Msb.) laEamoruka occurs in the Kur xv. 72, and means By thy life: (I'Ab, Akh, Bd, Jel:) and ↓ laEamaruka is a dial. var., mentioned by Yoo: (O:) or the former, accord. to the grammarians, means by thy religion: (AHeyth, O:) and [in like manner] laEamoriY , and ↓ laEamariY , [ by my life, or] by my religion. (K.) laEamoruka is an inchoative, of which the enunciative, maA A^uqosimu bihi , [ that by which I swear, so that the entire phrase means thy life is that by which I swear, ] is understood; therefore it is in the nom. case: (IJ, TA:) or the complete phrase is waEamorika falaEamoruka EaZiymN [ by thy life, &c.: and thy life is of great account ]. (Fr, as related by A'Obeyd.) You say also laEamoru A^abiyka Alxayora , and Alxayori ; the former meaning By thy father's instituting, or promoting, or keeping to, or observing, or regarding, what is good; Alxyr being the objective complement of Emr , from Eamara Alxayora , aor. , inf. n. EamorN and EimaArapN ; [see 1;] but in the latter case, Alxayori is an epithet added to A^abiyka [so that the meaning is by the life of thy good father ]. (AHeyth, Az, O, TA.) [See also art. xyr .] You also say laEamoru A@ll~`hi , meaning By the everlasting existence of God; (S, O, K;) Emr being here in the nom. case as an inchoative, with l prefixed to it as a corroborative of the inchoative state: the enunciative is understood; the complete phrase being laEamoru A@ll~`hi qasamiY or maA A^uqosimu bihi [ the everlasting existence of God is my oath, or that by which I swear ]. (S, O.) This expression is forbidden in a trad., (K,) because EamorN [properly] means the life of the body: (TA:) [but] laEamoru A_il`hika , meaning By the everlasting existence of thy God, occurs in a trad. (TA.) When you do not prefix l , you make it to be in the accus. case, as an inf. n.: thus you say, Emora A@ll~`hi maA faEalotu ka*aA (S, O, K) I swear by the everlasting existence of God, I did not so: (S, O:) and Eamoraka A@ll~`ha maA faEalotu ka*aA (S, O, K, [in the CK All~`hu , but this is a mistake,]) By thine acknowledgment of the everlasting existence of God, I did not so: (S, O:) or the original thereof is Eam~arotuka A@ll~`ha taEomiyrFA , (O, K,) i. e., I ask, or beg, God to prolong thy life: (Ks, O:) [and it is said in the S that Eamoraka A@ll~`ha sometimes has this signification:] and in like manner Eamoraka A@ll~`ha laA A^afoEalu *aAka means I beg God to prolong thy life: I will not do that: or it may be a form of oath without w [for waEamorika ]: (Ks:) and you say Eamoraka A@ll~`ha AifoEalo ka*aA and A_il~aA faEalota ka*aA [and A_il~aA maA faEalota ka*aA By thine acknowledgment of the everlasting existence of God, &c., do thou so ]: (TA:) or Eamoraka A@ll~`ha signifies by thy worship of God: (AHeyth:) or I remind thee, reminding thee, of God. (K.) Mbr says of this phrase, Emrk All~`h , that Emr may be in the accus. case on account of a verb understood; [such, for instance, as A^u*ak~iruka ;] or by reason of w suppressed, the complete phrase being waEamorika A@ll~`ha ; or as being for [the inf. n.] taEomiyr . (TA.) It may also be [found written] Eamora A@ll~`ha ; but this is bad. (Ks.) Some of the Arabs, for laEamoruka , said raEamoluka . (Az.) ― -b2- EamorFA wa$abaAbFA : see quHaAbN . -A2- EamorN (AHeyth, K) and ↓ EamarN (K) signify Religion; (AHeyth, K;) as in the phrases laEamoriY and ↓ laEamariY (K) and laEamoruka (AHeyth) [mentioned above]. -A3- Also EamorN (S, O, Msb, K) and ↓ EumorN (IAth, O, K) The flesh that is between the teeth: (S, O, Msb, K:) or the pendent piece of flesh between the teeth: (Az, Msb:) or the flesh that is between the places in which the teeth are set: (TA:) or the flesh of the gum: (K:) or the flesh of the gum that runs between any two teeth: (TA:) or what appears of the gum: (Kh, Msb:) or (so accord. to the TA, but in the K “ and ”) anything of an oblong shape between two teeth: (K:) pl. EumuwrN : (S, O, Msb, K:) which some explain as signifying the places whence the teeth grow. (TA.) It is said in a trad., A^awoSaAniY jiboriylu biAls~iwaAki Hat~aY xa$iytu EalaY EumuwriY [ Gabriel enjoined me to make use of the tooth-stick so that I feared for my Emwr ]. (O, TA.) -A4- A^um~u EamorKw : see EaAmirN .

definition: A visit, or a visiting: (S, Msb, K:) or a visit in which is the cultivation ( EimaArap ) of love or affection: (TA:) or a repairing to an inhabited, or a peopled, place: this is the primary signification.
sourceDefinition: A visit, or a visiting: (S, Msb, K:) or a visit in which is the cultivation ( EimaArap ) of love or affection: (TA:) or a repairing to an inhabited, or a peopled, place: this is the primary signification. (Mgh.) ― -b2- Hence the Eumorap in pilgrimage [and at any time]; (S, O; *) i. e. [ A religious visit to the sacred places at Mekkeh, with the performance of the ceremony of AlA_iHoraAm ,] the circuiting round the Kaabeh, and the going to and fro between Es-Safà and El-Marweh: AlHaj~u [differs from it inasmuch as it is at a particular time of the year and] is not complete without the halting at 'Arafát on the day of 'Arafeh: (Zj, TA:) the Eumorap is the minor pilgrimage ( AlHaj~u AlA^aSogaru ); (Msb, and Kull p. 168;) what is commonly termed AlHaj~u being called sometimes the greater pilgrimage ( AlHaj~u AlA^akobaru ): (Kull:) pl. EumarN (S, O, Msb) and EumaraAtN or EumuraAtN or EumoraAtN . (Msb.) ― -b3- Also A man's going in to his [ newlymarried ] wife in the abode of her family: (IAar, S, K:) if he removes her to his own family, the act is termed EurosN . (IAar, S.)

sourceDefinition: a subst., ( A_isomN [strangely read by Golius A^asomaru ], S, O,) or an inf. n., (TA,) [or rather a quasiinf. n.,] from A^aEomarahu daArFA and the like; (S, O, TA;) A man's assigning to another a house for the life of the latter, or for the life of the former; (accord. to the explanation of the verb in the K;) a man's saying to another, of a house, or of land, or of camels, It is thine, or they are thine, for my life, or for thy life, and when thou diest it returns, or they return, to me; (accord. to the explanation of the verb in the S and Mgh and O;) a man's giving to another a house, and saying to him, This is thine for thy life, or for my life: (Th, in TA: [in which is added, “ whichever of us dies, ” Ay~nA mAt , but this I consider a mistake for A_i*aA maAta , “ when he dies, ”) “ the house is given to his family: ”]) so they used to do in the Time of Ignorance: (TA:) but some of the Muslim lawyers hold the gift to be absolute, and the condition to be null. (TA, &c.) ― -b2- Also [The property, or house, &c., so given; ] what is assigned, or given, to another for the period of his life, or for that of the life of the giver. (K.) [See also ruqobaY .]

definition: Anything (AO, S, O, K) which one puts, (S, O,) or which a chief puts, (TA,) upon his head, such as a turban, and a qalanosuwap , and a crown, &c.
sourceDefinition: Anything (AO, S, O, K) which one puts, (S, O,) or which a chief puts, (TA,) upon his head, such as a turban, and a qalanosuwap , and a crown, &c., (AO, S, O, K,) as a sign of headship, and for keeping it in mind; (TA;) as also ↓ EamorapN (K) and ↓ EamaArN : (S, O, * TA:) which last [is app. a coll. gen. n., of which EamaArapN is the n. un., and] also signifies any sweet-smelling plant ( rayoHaAn ) which a chief puts upon his head for the same purpose: and hence, (tropical:) any such plant, absolutely: (B:) or any such plant with which a drinkingchamber is adorned, (S, K,) called by the Persians mayowaraAno ; when any one comes in to the people there assembled, they raise somewhat thereof with their hands, and salute him with it, wishing him a long life: so, accord. to some, in a verse of El-Aashà, which see below: (S:) or it there signifies crowns of such plants, which they put upon their heads, as the foreigners ( AlEajam ) do; but ISd says, “ I know not how this is: ” or the myrtle; syn. A=s : (TA:) and EamaArpN signifies a plant of that kind, with which one used to salute a king, saying, May God prolong thy life: or, as some say, a raising of the voice, saying so: (Az, TA:) a salutation; (K;) said to mean, may God prolong thy life; (TA;) as also ↓ EamaArN (S, K) and ↓ EimaArapN ; (L;) but Az says that this explanation is not valid. (TA.) El-Aashà says, falam~aA A^ataAnaA buEayoda AlkaraY ↓ sajadonaA lahu warafaEonaA AlEamaAraA [ And when he came to us, a little after slumber, we prostrated ourselves to him, and ] we put the turbans from our heads, in honour of him: (S:) but IB says that, accord. to this explanation, the correct reading is waDaEonaA AlEamaAraA : (TA:) or the former reading means, we raised our voices with prayer for him, and said, May God prolong thy life: or we raised the sweet-smelling plants: &c.: see above. (S, TA.) ― -b2- Also EamaArapN , (K,) or ↓ EimaArapN , (O,) An ornamented piece of cloth which is sewed upon a miZ~l~ap , [by which is meant a kind of tent, ] (O, K, TA,) i. e. sewed to the Tariyqap [q. v.], on each side of the tent-pole, (O,) as a sign of headship. (TA.) -A2- See also EimaArapN .

EamaAy^iru . (TA.) -A3- See also EamaArapN , in two places.

sourceDefinition: Living long. (Msb, TA.) ― -b2- Remaining, continuing, staying, residing, dwelling, or abiding, in a place: (TA:) and thus, or remaining, &c., and congregated, in a pl. sense. (Mus'ab, O.) [Hence,] An inhabitant of a house: pl. Eum~aArN . (TA.) And Eum~aAru Albuyuwti The jinn, or genii, that inhabit houses. (S.) And EawaAmiru Albuyuwti The serpents that are in houses: sing. EaAmirN and EaAmirapN : accord. to some, they are so called because of the length of their lives. (TA.) ― -b3- See also muEotamirN . -A2- Also i. q. ↓ maEomwrN . (O, TA.) [See also EumoraAnN .] You say A^aroDN EaAmirapN A land peopled; [ colonized; cultivated; &c. ] (TA.) [See Eamara .] And manozilN EaAmirN A place of abode inhabited [&c.]. (Msb.) And makaAnN EaAmirN , and ↓ EamiyrN , (S, O, TA,) i. e. *uw EimaArapK [ A place inhabited, peopled, well stocked with people and the like, in a flourishing state, in a state the contrary of desolate or waste or ruined ]. (TA.) ― -b2- It is applied also to that which has been a ruin or waste or the like [as meaning In a state of good repair; in a state the contrary of ruined or waste or desolate ]; and so ↓ maEomuwrN . (S, TA.) [Pl. EumoraAnN .] -A3- A_in~ahu laEaAmirN lirab~ihi Verily he is a server, or worshipper, of his Lord. (TA.) -A4- A^um~u EaAmirK , (S, O, K,) and ↓ A^um~u EamorKw , (K,) but the latter is extr., (TA,) The hyena; (S, O, K;) a metonymical surname, (S, O,) determinate, as applying to the species. (TA.) It is said in a prov., xaAmirY A^um~a EaAmiri A^abo$iriY bijaraAdK EaZolaY wakamari rijaAlK qatolaY [ Hide thyself, O Umm-'Ámir: rejoice thou at the news of locusts cohering, and the glands of the penes of slain men: (in this prov., for kam~i , in the TA, I have substituted kamarK , which is the reading in variations of the prov.: see Freytag's Arab. Prov., i. 431:)] this being said by a man, [it is asserted that] the animal becomes obsequious to him, so that he muzzles it, and then drags it forth; for the hyena, says Az, is proverbial for its stupidity, and for its being beguiled with soft speech. (TA.) It is called Am~ EAmr , as though its young one were called EaAmirN , and it is so called by a Hudhalee poet: (L:) or its whelp is called AlEaAmiru : (K:) but it is not known with Al in the compound name with the prefixed noun [ Am~ , nor, app., without Am~ ]. (MF, from the Expos. of the dur~ap .)

definition: A state, condition, or case.
sourceDefinition: A state, condition, or case. (S, O, K.) So in the saying, naEima Eawofuka [ May thy state, &c., be good, or pleasant ]. (S, O.) One says also, A^aSobaHa fulaAnN biEawofi sawo'K , and biEawofi xayorK , meaning [ Such a one entered upon the morning, or, simply, became, ] in an evil state, and in a good state: or, accord. to some of the lexicologists, one should not say biEawofi xayorK , but only $ar~K [or sawo'K ]. (IDrd, O.) ― -b2- Also Fortune; syn. jad~N and HaZ~N . (O, K.) And so, accord. to some, in the saying, naEima Eawofuka [i. e. May thy fortune be good ]. (O, TA.) ― -b3- And i. q. TaAy^irN [as meaning An omen ]. (K, TA.) And thus it is said to signify in the form of prayer above mentioned: (TA:) [for,] as some say, the meaning is, naEima Tayoruka [ May thy omen be good ]. (O, TA.) ― -b4- And The *akar . (O, K.) One says to a man on the morning after his first going in to his wife, naEima Eawofuka , meaning thereby the *akar [i. e. May thy *kr be in a good state ]. (O, TA.) A'Obeyd says, Some men used to explain ( yataA^aw~alu [for which yatanaAwalu is erroneously put in the O]) AlEawof as the faroj [meaning the *akar ], and I mentioned it to AA, and he disapproved it: (S, O, TA:) but a verse has been cited in which EawofiY [certainly] means *akariY . (TA.) ― -b5- And A guest. (Lth, O, K.) And thus it has been expl. as used in the saying, naEima Eawofuka . (O, * TA.) ― -b6- And The cock. (O, K.) ― -b7- And The lion: because he seeks his prey (↓ yataEaw~afu ) by night. (O, K.) ― -b8- And The wolf. (O, K.) ― -b9- And One who toils, or seeks the means of subsistence, for his household, or family. (IAar, O, K.) ― -b10- And A certain idol. (O, K.) ― -b11- And A species of trees; (O;) or a species of plants, (AHn, O, K,) of the plants of the desert, (AHn, O,) of sweet odour. (AHn, O, K.) ― -b12- A^um~u EawofK The jaraAdap , (S, O,) [i. e.] the female of the jaraAd [or locust ]. (K.) And A^abuw EawofK The jaraAd [meaning the male locust ]. (Az, O, K.) -A2- Also (i. e. EawofN ) a good manner of tending or pasturing [cattle]: (O, K:) [or rather, simply,] the tending or pasturing [cattle]: so in the saying, A_in~ahu laHasanu AlEawofi fiY A_ibilihi [ Verily he is one who has a good quality of tending, or pasturing, in respect of his camels ]. (TA.)

definition: A dense, or tangled wood;
sourceDefinition: A dense, or tangled wood; a numerous collection of dense, or tangled, trees: (S, O, K:) or [ lote-trees of the species called ] sidor (AHn, O, TA) collected together in one place, (AHn, O,) of which the lower parts are dense, or tangled: (AHn, TA:) or dense, or tangled, trees, some growing in, or among, the lower parts of others: (TA:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aEoyaASN and [of mult.] EiSoyAnN : (O, K:) also what are collected together (AHn, O, K, TA) in a place, (AHn, O, TA,) and are near together, and dense, or tangled, (AHn, O, K, TA,) of [ trees of the kinds called ] EiDaAh , (O, K,) or of [ the trees called ] sidor and Eawosaj and naboE and salam and all kinds of EDAh : so says 'Omárah, (O, TA,) and AHn says the like: (TA:) or (K) what are dense, or tangled, and numerous, (El-Kilábee, O, TA,) of thick and tough trees, (El-Kilábee, O, K, TA,) such as the salam and TaloH and sayaAl and sidor and samur and EurofuT and EiDaAh . (El-Kilábee, O, TA.) ― -b2- Also A place of growth of the best of trees: (Lth, A, O, K:) or, as some say, the lower parts of trees. (TA.) ― -b3- And hence, (A,) A stock, or race. (S, * A, K. *) You say, huwa mino EiySi baniY haA$imK He is of the stock, or race, of Benoo-Háshim. (A.) And maA A^akorama EiySahu How generous, or noble, are his fathers, or ancestors, and paternal and maternal uncles, and the people of his house ! (TA.) And it is said in a prov., EiySuka minoka waA_ino kaAna A^a$ibFA , i. e. Thy stock is an appertenance of thine though it be thorny and intricate or confused: (AZ, O, TA:) meaning, accord. to A'Obeyd, those who are connected with thee by origin are thy kinsmen, although they follow a different way of life: have patience, therefore, for thou canst not remove them from thee: (Meyd:) [see Freytag's Arab. Prov., ii. 95:] implying dispraise: or, accord. to AHeyth, EiySN A^a$ibN denotes praise; force of resistance, or inaccessibleness or unapproachableness, and numerousness, being meant thereby. (O, TA.) You say also, huwa fiY EiySi SidoqK He is of a good, or an excellent, stock. (Sh, O, TA.) ― -b4- jiy^o bihi mino EiySika means Bring thou it from wherever it is. (TA.)

definition: The nineteenth letter of the alphabet: called gayonN .
sourceDefinition: The nineteenth letter of the alphabet: called gayonN . It is one of the letters termed Haloqiy~ap [or faucial], (L, TA,) its place of utterance being the upper part of the fauces, near to that of H , (TA in art. gyn ,) the same place as that of x , (L, TA,) [from which it differs in being pronounced with the voice, for] it is of the letters termed majohuwrap [or vocal], (L, TA, and K in art. gyn ,) and of those that are termed musotaEoliyap [q. v.]; one should not reiterate the voice in uttering it, so as to exceed what is right, nor neglect exactness in respect of its place of utterance, so as to render it obscure, but should make it thoroughly distinct, and clear: it is not an augmentative letter: and [it is said that] it is not substituted [for another letter]: (K in art. gyn :) [but this is a mistake; for] it is substituted for two letters; for x , in gaTara biyadihi , aor. yagoTiru , meaning xaTara , aor. yaxoTiru , mentioned by IJ and several others, (MF, TA,) and in gaTara bi*anabihi for xaTara ; (TA in art. xTr ;) and for E , in lagan~a for laEan~a , mentioned by Ibn-Umm- Kásim and others, (MF, TA,) [and in na$uwgN for na$uwgN ,] and in Airomagal~a for AiromaEal~a , and also in Algayonu as signifying “ thirst ” and “ the clouds. ” (TA in art. gyn .) -A2- [As a numeral, it denotes A thousand. ]

definition: , (S,) or AlmaA$iyapu , (Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S,) or AlmaA$iyapu , (Msb, K,) aor. , inf. n. gab~N (S, Msb, K) and gubuwbN , (Msb, K,) The camels, (S,) or cattle, (Msb, K,) came to water, (S,) or drank, (Msb, K,) on alternate days; one day and not the next day. (S, Msb, K.) ― -b2- Hence, (IAth, TA,) gab~a said of a man means He came visiting at intervals of some days, or after some days. (AA, IAth, TA.) [See also gib~N : and see gubayosN .] ― -b3- And gab~a Eani Alqawomi , (Ks, S, Msb, K,) aor. , the verb in this case being of the class of qatala , [but this is contr. to analogy, as well as to the derivation,] inf. n. gib~N , with kesr, He came to the people, or party, day after day: (Msb:) or, as also Alqawoma ↓ Agb~ , he came to the people, or party, on alternate days, coming one day and not the next: (Ks, S, K:) or he came to them once in two days or more. (TA.) It is said in a trad., fiY EiyaAdapi AlmariyDi ↓ A^agib~uwA waA^arobiEuwA Visit ye the sick on alternate days and after intervals of two days: (S, TA:) not every day, lest he find your visits to be troublesome. (TA. [See also art. rbE .]) And you say, ↓ A^agobabotuhu , inf. n. A_igobaAbN , meaning I visited him [ once ] in every week. (A.) ― -b4- And hence gab~ato said of a fever. (Msb.) gab~ati AlHum~aY and ↓ A^agab~at signify the same: (S:) you say, gab~ato Ealayohi AlHum~aY , The fever came upon him, (Msb,) or attacked him, (K,) one day and intermitted one day; (Msb, K;) as also ↓ A^agab~atohu and ↓ A^agab~ato Ealayohi . (K.) [See also gib~N .] ― -b5- You say also, gab~a EinodanaA , (S, L, K,) and ↓ Agb~ , (L, K,) He passed the night, or a night, at our abode. (S, L, K.) Hence the saying, ruwayoda Al$~iEora yagib~a [so accord. to the TA, Hat~aY being understood, accord. to the explanation of Meyd, but in the CK, and in one of my copies of the S, and in Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 522, yagib~u ,] (S, K,) i. e. Leave thou the poetry until some days shall have passed, that thou mayest see what will be its result, whether it will be praised or dispraised: (Meyd, TA:) or it may be from gab~at said of a fever, and may thus mean, leave thou the poetry to be kept back from people, [or to be intermitted, ] i. e. do not repeat it to people in an uninterrupted manner, lest they become weary. (Meyd. [See also art. rwd .]) ― -b6- And [hence] gab~a , (T, S, L, Msb, K,) aor. , (L, Msb,) inf. n. gab~N and gib~N and gubuwbN and gubuwbapN , (L,) said of food, (L, Msb,) and of dates, or especially of flesh-meat as some say, (L,) It remained throughout a night, whether it became corrupt or not: (L, Msb:) and, said of food, it became altered [ for the worse ] in its odour: (L:) or, said of flesh-meat, it became stinking: (T, S, K;) as also ↓ Agb~ : (T, K:) and it (a thing) became corrupt. (TA. [See also 2.]) ― -b7- gab~ati AlA^umuwru means The affairs, or events, came to, or arrived at, their ends, conclusions, latter or last parts or states, issues, or results. (S, TA.) ― -b8- And gab~a Al$~ay^ou fiY nafosihi , aor. , inf. n. gab~N , [app. meaning The thing came into his mind, ] is a phrase mentioned by Th. (TA.)

One says, zuro gib~FA tazodado Hub~FA [or, accord. to common usage, Hib~FA , to assimilate it to gib~FA , Visit once a week, or at intervals of some days; not frequently, or not every day: so thou shalt have more love: a prov., respecting which see Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 587; where gub~FA is put for gib~FA ]. (S, O.) [See another ex. voce taraj~ala , last sentence.] The saying of Zeyd-el-Fawáris yaraAniY AlEaduw~u baEoda gib~i liqaAy^ihi means [ The enemy will see me ] after the day of meeting with him by a day.
